For almost two hundred years past, as we can gather both by conjecture and from the writings of those before us, the purity of monastic observance in this monastery of Spanheim, as in almost all others, failed, and the disorderly life of the monks utterly squandered all temporal substance. For indeed, when in the year of the Christians 1469 [unclear].
Frederick, duke of Bavaria, reformed the monastery of Spanheim.

Consider now, therefore, your calling, O monks, and do not corrupt your purpose of holiness, if you desire to arrive at the glory of God. Woe to you, faithless monk, who, having become a despiser of your calling and a transgressor of your vow, live in the monastery not as a monk: you who were called to endure tribulation patiently for the love of God, and yet ask about refreshment.

For your profession commands you to be humbly content with all mean and very poor clothing, and you are not afraid to devote your zeal to finery in dress. You were called to thirst, and you, despising the drinking of water, delight in drinking wine to satiety, against the monastic rule. You were made a monk to fight bravely against the enemy of your salvation, and you, throwing away from yourself the weapons of the virtues, go about lazy, idle, and naked; indeed, what is worse, with a troop of vices accompanying you. You were invited to watch in holy prayers, and you are dissolved in sluggish sleep and shameful idleness. You were called into the subjection of humble obedience, and you, swollen with pride, despise obedience to the precepts of your elders. You were called into charity, and you do not fear to carry hatred against your brother in your breast. You were called to weeping and tears, and you pour out laughter with disorderly guffawing.

The Lord called you to repentance in the monastery, and you, loosened into wantonness, join sin to sin. You were called to meditate day and night on the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you, walking after vanity, devote yourself to tales and perishable things. You were called to heaven, and you, loving the world, pursue earthly things. The Lord called you into the meekness of humility, and you go about full of rancor and pride. You were called by the Lord to the perfection of the purest monastic way of life, and you rot away like a beast in the dung of vanity and negligence. You were called to the observance of God’s commandments, and you, given over to the pleasures of the flesh, think of nothing less than Christ. You were invited to love the Lord Jesus above all things, and you walk after the evil desires of your heart, showing yourself ungrateful to your Redeemer. You who ought to have lived by the Spirit savor earthly things, and, drowned in pride, you despise all the holy exercises of the spiritual life.

And what will you answer on that day of judgment to the Judge, who will say to you, most ungrateful one: I, who am Lord of all things, humbled myself for your sake, taking the form of a servant, and, being found in appearance as a man, poured out my blood for you; for you I endured scourges, and for you I underwent a most bitter death of my own free will. I, O monk, loved you with my whole heart; I redeemed you by my blood from everlasting death; I called you out of love to the heavenly kingdom, if you had kept my commandments. But you lived contrary to my precepts, and, what is worse, though you had sworn yourself to my words, you were not afraid to show yourself against me, your Lord, as an apostate, impious traitor. Now

Therefore give an account of your stewardship. What then will you answer, O lazy and idle monk, who now spends the present acceptable time so fruitlessly, and despises living in true monastic purity according to the rule? What, I ask, will you answer? Will you deny the works of wickedness that you have committed, intending by deceit to show good works that you now disdain to perform, so that, deceiving the Judge by a lie, you may thus escape the punishment due to your demerits?

But you must not be ignorant that everything you have done, said, or thought throughout your whole life, good and evil alike, is manifest in the sight of the Judge, and nothing can be hidden from him who alone knows all things. For all things are written in the book of God, and your conscience will bear open testimony against you concerning all the evils you have done, so that not even the smallest thought will be able to lie hidden. For the Scripture of the prophets says to God in Psalm 75: “For the thought of man shall confess to you.”

You are to be judged before the tribunal of the all-knowing one, before whose terrible judgment every creature will stand in great fear and trembling, where no excuse whatever is admitted, but each person will receive the sentence due to his merits, with appeal set aside. Thousands of thousands and ten hundred thousand holy spirits will stand beside him, and do you trust that you can deceive the Judge by a lie?

But hear my counsel, and, rising from your destructive inertia, at last wake up, and by true repentance flee in time from justice to the mercy of God. Do not put it off from day to day, because it is extremely dangerous for one remaining in sins to be confident, and to reject the remedy of salvation that is offered. Remember that you are going to die, and when you do not expect it, you will be summoned to judgment.

Consider, I beg you, how the uncertain time of life slips away, and how quickly all mortal things decay. Nothing among human affairs is stable, nothing fixed, nothing firm; rather all things that we see are corruptible and change with time. Consider also where our brothers Valentinus, Martinus, and Ioannes are, who in the present year were living with us healthy, safe, and joyful; they spoke with us, ate, drank, and labored together with us, thinking of nothing less than that they would die this year. Behold, when they did not think it, death came, snatched them away, and set their souls before the tribunal of the dreadful Judge, who rendered to each one according to the works of his hands.

Behold, now learn from the example of your brothers that you too are going to die, and perhaps you will pass from this world much sooner than you can estimate. Come to your senses, wretched man, while you still can; do penance in the time of your health, while the Judge promises mercy, and do not defer today’s good into tomorrow’s uncertainty. Rise up, even now, late though it is, at last from the sloth of your more negligent past way of life, in which until now you have shamefully rotted away; cleanse your conscience from every stain of sin; wipe away with tears the evil you have committed, and from now on live innocently, as befits a monk.

Take up a firm purpose of complete amendment, and understand that the kingdom of heaven is promised not to those who begin well, but to those who persevere to the end. Know also that heaven is not reached by idleness and sluggishness, but by great labor, by the strongest effort of the will to make progress, and by tireless zeal in spiritual exercise.

Therefore, wishing to serve and please the Lord, always stand in the truth within yourself, fearful in awe, and prepare your soul for temptation. The disordered impulses and desires of the flesh must be strongly resisted; all the enticements and vanities of the world must be fought against with a most steadfast spirit; through prayers and greatness of soul the devil, the adversary of our salvation, must be driven away.

No sleepy, lazy, slothful person ever reached the kingdom of God; no one without continual labor and much sweat has obtained heaven. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent,” that is, those who have learned steadfastly to resist the evil desires of the flesh, “seize it.” Review the deeds of all the saints, and nowhere will you find anyone sanctified without great and continual labor. For even if no one becomes holy by his own powers, nevertheless the gracious mercy of the almighty Lord, which grants to those who strive both the will to do good and the strength, sanctifies no one without the works of a good and upright will.

Since, then, God wills all men to be saved and no one to perish, we, my brothers, must take the greatest care not to receive his grace in vain, but rather strive with all our strength, so that, like fertile soil, we may always answer the free gifts of so great a sower with fitting fruits from the works of a good will.

Let us therefore arm ourselves with the shield of faith, and put on the breastplate of steadfastness and saving patience, so that, prepared against everything that can happen to us, through humility and the fervor of the Holy Spirit, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, we may overcome. In all these things patience is very necessary for us; without its support there never has been, nor could there ever be, perseverance in good and holy works. For there was no other way to heaven for the saints than patience; nor could anyone ever be sanctified who cast patience aside.

Indeed, all who have pleased almighty God from the beginning of the world down to this our age have triumphed over the prince of the world in no other way than through patience. Hence all of them could most rightly say that verse of the psalmist: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” The most holy apostle of Christ, Paul, also recalling the patience of the saints of old, says among other things: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves, and in the caverns of the earth.” For all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, because, as the prophet says, “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.”
On patience and gentleness.

Patience, therefore, is necessary for all mortals, and it especially befits those who live in the cloister, since, just as adversities are never lacking to the righteous in this world, so no one will be justified without patience. Now the principal degrees of patience, as the diligence of the ancients distinguished them, are three.

The first and lowest is that of those people who neither seek out adversities nor bear them willingly, but when they befall them are weighed down in spirit and cast down with sorrow; they also sometimes complain and murmur for a time against those who inflict them. But after the agitation of their inflamed mind has passed, they return to themselves, and seem patiently to endure the insult inflicted on them without revenge. Yet the patience of these people, not being of great virtue, is always very near the fault of an unquiet mind, and therefore is often to be reckoned of no merit, and sometimes of lesser merit. And although in our times such people are called distinguished by the virtue of patience, nevertheless, compared with the holy men of old, they do not deserve this venerable name of Christian long-suffering and endurance. For that does not seem to be true patience which has been darkened by bitterness and indignation of an agitated mind.

The second degree of patience is said to belong to those people who, although they do not seek to suffer evils, nevertheless, when they come, receive them freely and kindly, and embrace them most patiently as though they were a gift sent by God. Such people are truly to be called patient: inflamed with divine love, they bear with equanimity whatever adversity has occurred, and preserve, even in tribulation, the same tranquillity of mind that they formerly had in prosperity. I would not doubt that that most holy Idumaean Job was of their number: struck not only by extreme adversity, he bore all things patiently, but even when placed in the whirlpool of evils, he gave thanks and blessed the Lord, saying: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

All Christians ought to keep this degree of patience, and especially, before others, those who live in the cloister. For the wise man says: “A man’s learning is known through patience.” For the more learned anyone is in the law of the Lord and in the knowledge of the ordering of rational nature, the more patient he will be in adversities. What if I, as a lover of truth, speak more boldly: that adversities profit us more than prosperities, if we are learned and not forgetful weighers of our own condition?

The third degree of patience, surely the highest and most perfect of the remaining ones, is rightly granted to those who not only, when there is need, bear adversities with equanimity for the love of God and the benefit of the brethren, but who also, inflamed with a more fervent spirit of charity, willingly thrust themselves forward and hasten eagerly to receive insults and injuries. And this kind of patience is divided in two ways, just as a twofold manner of martyrdom of the saints is found. For some, when they could have lain hidden during the persecution of believers, with the charity of Christ burning in them, with no one compelling them, but of their own free will, presented themselves to the tribunals of their persecutors [unclear].
Homily XVIII.

[unclear], and, publicly confessing Jesus as Redeemer of the world, they received the tortures inflicted on them with joy. Others, although they did not offer themselves of their own accord, nevertheless willingly received the martyrdom offered to them, always ready to endure for the faith of Christ whatever the cruelty of tyrants could have inflicted.

The most radiant Confessors rightly hold a rank nearer to these; even if the cruelty of the impious did not take them away by persecution, still they in no way lost the glory of martyrdom. For by crucifying their flesh in this world for the name of Christ, they endured a voluntary and long-lasting martyrdom: through abstinence and humility they were made glorious, steadfast in soul, always most patient, and most ready to undergo martyrdom bodily.

Take care, O monks, to be imitators of them according to your strength, so that, since enemies who kill the body for Christ are now lacking, you may show yourselves martyrs in mind and spirit by resisting the desires of the flesh and patiently enduring adversities for the love of God. In the peace of the saints, the best kind of martyrdom is to afflict the flesh for God’s name through abstinence, to desire nothing in this world, always to advance in good works, and, if any evil happens, to bear it in all things gladly and patiently with cheerfulness of mind.

Live henceforth according to this rule of patience, dearest brothers, if you desire to reign with Christ forever. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ, so that each one may cheerfully give to his brother what he desires to be done for himself.
In this way all Christians owe martyrdom to Christ.
On the True Humility of Monks. Homily XIX.

It is the judgment of almost all the teachers, dearest brothers, that the highest and chief virtue of monks is no other than humility, because it is itself the mother and nurse of all virtues. For humility makes the monk; pride destroys and corrupts him. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor little one, and the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words?”

For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, because pride is the beginning of every sin, and without true humility no one can attain salvation. Since this is so, I think it necessary, brothers, to exhort you without ceasing that, fleeing pride, you always preserve deep humility in all your works. Indeed, no good work is believed to please the Lord God if it is presented without the seasoning of humility.

For humility is a most healthful medicine for the souls of the faithful, helping all, because it presses down the swollen inward parts of the spirit, restores what is wasting away, corrects what is depraved, and removes what has grown excessive. O humility, mother and parent of all virtues: you strengthen patience, stir up compunction, illumine charity, adorn chastity, make prayer fruitful [unclear].

You give [unclear], and commend fasting and abstinence. O holy humility, truly beloved of God, through repentance you justify the ungodly; you preserve the just man in his resolve of holiness; you powerfully open heaven to those who love you; you close hell to the penitent.

O venerable humility, exceedingly pleasing to God, you compelled the Son of the eternal Father to descend from heaven into the womb of Mary, the most chaste and perpetual Virgin. You made him appear visible to us; you laid him, wrapped in poor cloths, in a manger, so that he might adorn us in heaven with the ornaments of everlasting happiness. You drove the Son of God to undergo circumcision of the flesh, so that we, circumcised in mind, might be able to enter the promised inheritance of the saints.

O humility of great power, you made the King of heaven and earth withdraw before the face of one most contemptible little man, and dwell in seven years’ exile in the land of Egypt. You made Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, whom you compelled to assume a human body for our salvation, undergo also his most bitter passion and death by his own free will.

Great is your dominion, O venerable humility of holiness, since the kingdom of heaven is promised to you, the gift of everlasting blessedness is granted to your worshipers, and whoever keeps to your footsteps is raised up to the height of the angels, as Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled; and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” The King of heaven taught you, when he said to his imitators: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” The most blessed Mother of God also, the untouched Virgin Mary, speaks thus of the Lord God in her sweetest song of praise: “He has cast down the mighty from their seats and exalted the humble.” And the prophet says in the psalm: “The Lord has regarded the prayers of the humble, and has not despised their petitions.” For the prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the clouds; until it draws near, he will not be comforted, and he will not depart until the Most High looks upon him.

Humility makes a monk who is pure in his conscience most pleasing to God; and the more he casts himself down by humbling himself for God’s honor, the more glorious he will appear in the kingdom. The monk who truly humbles himself becomes a son of the Most High through participation in grace, and will rejoice forever with the King of heaven, Jesus Christ.

He who truly desires to imitate Christ should also take up true humility; girded and protected by it as by a breastplate of strength, he will do great things, thinking nothing of himself except what is humble, and will not incur the stain of vainglory. For this is the true perfection of monks: always humbly to recognize their own imperfection, and diligently to consider rather what good is lacking to them than what they possess.

For true humility always stretches forward toward the things ahead through the desire of charity; mindful of what is past, it fears lest it lose what it has, and, desiring to acquire through the zeal of devotion what it does not yet have, it does not grow lukewarm in the fervor of holiness. It considers most carefully how greatly it is still deficient, and in what respects it has made progress [unclear].

Indeed, whoever already thinks himself to be something is still farther from true humility, since true humility does great things and thinks the least of itself; and the more it has advanced, the more deeply it recognizes its own weakness. For so Scripture has instructed us, saying: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God.” And again it says: “Humble your spirit greatly, for the punishment of the flesh of the ungodly is fire and the worm.”

Therefore, my brothers, take up true humility: not that which is sometimes displayed outwardly in gesture and voice before men by pretenders, but Christian humility, which is possessed by the pure affection of the heart. For it is one thing to have the virtue of humility, and another to have the appearance of its likeness. True humility is always patient with a tranquil heart toward every injury and insult; it is obedient without dispute to commands, not only of superiors but even of equals; in adversities it preserves constancy, in bodily necessity moderation, in conduct a good conscience, in common life honorableness. It is cheerful, not dissolute; serious, not melancholy; generous in acts of mercy, not wasteful; compassionate toward the weak, not lax.

Christian humility is unceasingly pierced with compunction in the love of God; fervent in the spirit of devotion, it is continually watered with tears; it always longs to see its prince, Jesus Christ, and, following his admonitions in spirit, sighs from grief. For whoever embraces true humility grieves that he is a sinner; whoever imitates the Son of God groans that he cannot advance as much as he desires.

Nothing is more excellent than Christian humility, nothing more splendid than self-knowledge, which, though always set in a higher place, is never exalted, and, though subject to all, rules over all. For he who is small in his own eyes becomes great before God; and he who thinks himself to be something great in this world is judged before God to be of no account. For each person will be the more precious before the inward judge, the more, while doing good and never failing, he has been contemptible in his own estimation.

Humility is the stable foundation of all virtues, since every spiritual building that is raised up to the height of Christian perfection is supported by the rock of humility alone. Indeed, if true humility is lacking, the gathering of the other virtues will be nothing but the collapse of a house built without a foundation on sand. For in the spiritual building humility lays the stable foundation; charity orders the breadth of that house; the wall is raised on high by the continuation of good works in fervor of spirit; the roof is set at the top in faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and in firm hope of the promise of eternal protection and happiness; and the length is arranged in the long-suffering of patience with most beautiful order.
Therefore, my brothers, again and again I admonish, entreat, and beg you to take care to found the building of spiritual exercise in the depth of humility, since

No good work pleases God if it has been offered apart from true humility. There are, moreover, many things that are accustomed to stir the servants of God to true humility. For some are humbled before God within themselves by consideration of their own vileness, because, when they consider that they have now often experienced themselves to be wretched and weak, they place all their hope and confidence, in humility, in God. Others, carefully weighing the multitude of God’s benefits toward them, fear the judgment due to ingratitude, and therefore they always walk humbly in the sight of God with great fear and reverent gratitude.

And which of us, brothers, is there to whom the mercy of almighty God has not granted many benefits, even in a special way? If we wish to be grateful to him, we must above all be humble. Others, after a multitude of sins, having been turned by divine kindness to repentance, diligently recall to memory how many evils they have committed against the law of the Almighty, and for these, humbled in bitterness of spirit, they detest their impieties with horror.

But we offend in many things; therefore it is necessary that we humble ourselves always in mind and also outwardly in body, so that grace may abound where sin previously abounded. Often, indeed, the providence of divine mercy permits certain people to sin grievously for a time, so that afterward, when they have been converted to repentance, they may learn to remain in true humility. Better is a humble penitent than a proud man who has not sinned, since humility justifies penitents, and pride condemns the arrogant forever, even if they have done nothing else wrong than this alone, that they are proud.

Others, bearing in their heart through daily meditation the bitter passion of Christ Jesus, humble themselves all the more, the more they know that they are far too insufficient as debtors for such great and wondrous benefits of their Redeemer. The Son of God humbled himself, becoming man for us, and, filled with many reproaches, voluntarily underwent the most shameful death of the cross, so that he might free us from the destruction of perpetual death. What Christian man, and especially what monk, will not greatly humble his soul before God when he recalls to memory such humility of his Creator and Redeemer?

Indeed, the man whom the humility of Christ does not stir to meekness will not be helped by any admonitions of men. We are called monks in vain unless, according to our strength, we have humbly followed Christ. For this reason he said in the holy Gospel that he himself is the way, so that we may imitate his humility, and so that the way of life of so great a Master may become the spiritual pattern of the disciple. Therefore we, brothers, must strive with all our strength, as much as we can, so that humility, conceived through meditation on the most bitter passion of Jesus Christ, may level, restore, and reform everything in us that pride has made swollen.

Oh, how fitting it is for us to humble our souls for the love of Jesus Christ, my brothers, when God himself, the Creator of all things, made man, cast himself down into such humility for us. The chief medicine, then, for inducing true humility in God’s servant is if...

daily, and more often, recalls to memory the most bitter passion of Christ Jesus. Tribulations, adversities, and illnesses, together with poverty or want, have also made many humble, who perhaps in prosperity and good fortune would have perished through pride. And we trust, as we shall often say, that poverty contributes to our salvation, since we have in it a great cause for humility, while we find no matter at all for self-exaltation and pride. Others, through the continual practice of virtues and the remembrance of death, which they must shortly and inevitably undergo, have come to great humility.

Whom, however proud, would not earnest meditation on death humble? Or who is so fierce in spirit that he would not little by little lay aside his swelling pride, if he considered more carefully that he would die in a short time? Therefore the conscience of a monk must never drive away from itself the memory of future death, so that he may remain both humble and sorrowful: that, standing firm in humility, he may not grow proud, and that continual grief may forbid every wantonness to the heart.

Some also the gracious mercy of God forestalls, and by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit makes humble. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God utterly detests pride. He who truly knows himself is most wise, and cannot depart from the meekness of humility. But every proud and arrogant man is ignorant, even if he seems great and renowned among mortals. For true wisdom rests in the dwelling-place of holy humility, and is shown more clearly through the proof of patience.

From the knowledge of God and of oneself humility is born, and this is rightly called true wisdom. He who has truly known himself now has nothing from which to grow proud, because, knowing his own vileness, he thinks nothing lofty, but, set in sorrow of soul, cries to the Lord: “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you regard him? Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow.” Why then is earth and ashes proud? Why does the spirit of frail and mortal man swell up against God?

Be humbled, therefore, my dearest brothers, as it is written, under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation. For humility with chaste fear is highly pleasing to the Lord God in his servants, since without it he approves no virtue of man for salvation. Therefore, if we desire to climb the throne of the lofty kingdom of heaven, we must be very humble, because there is no other way to heaven except that of deepest humility, by which the Son of God himself and all the saints ascended. But all who have tried to enter the kingdom by another gate, striking the head of pride against the threshold of humility, have been wholly unable to enter. For the gate of humility does not admit the proud, and the narrow way of meekness does not receive lovers of avarice and self-exaltation. Therefore whoever desires to come to the height of the heavenly kingdom must ascend by the steps of humility; without them, whoever begins to ascend falls into the depth of perdition and death.

he undoubtedly falls. For humility is the ladder to heaven, beautifully divided into twelve degrees; concerning its ascent our lawgiver Benedict says in the Rule: “If we wish to reach the summit of highest humility and swiftly arrive at that heavenly exaltation, we must set up for ourselves that ladder which appeared to Jacob in his dream, by which angels were shown to him ascending and descending.” Without doubt that descent and ascent are understood by us to mean nothing other than descending by exaltation and ascending by humility, as divine Scripture shows us: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted.” The ladder itself, set upright, is our life in this world, which, when the heart is humbled, is raised up by the Lord into heaven. For we say that the sides of this ladder are our body and soul; into these sides the divine summons has inserted the different steps of humility and discipline that must be climbed. He then follows and enumerates those twelve steps in order, with a sufficiently beautiful arrangement; since they are altogether very well known to you, it would be superfluous to spend longer on reviewing them this time.

It is enough in this place to remember the holy canon, in whose words you all long ago swore voluntarily, so that you may know that humility is no less necessary for salvation than love of God and of neighbor alike. For humility is said to be the monk’s greatest virtue, and it is so necessary to his profession that without it he cannot be saved. A monk who is puffed up in spirit and proud is not the servant of Christ, but the slave of the devil; he will have no share with the Son of God in heaven, but will be tormented without end with the demons in hell. For Christ, the teacher and forerunner of humility, detests all the proud and admits none into his fellowship except the humble, the meek, and the gentle. But the devil is the head and inventor of pride; all who follow his pride and arrogance are his servants and disciples. For he himself, the king of the proud, cannot endure humility; he flees the meek and does not dare to stand in the sight of the gentle in heart.

For Christ dwells in the assembly of the humble servants of God; but in the midst of the proud the devil stirs up contentions and the quarrels of those at odds. Where humility is, there is true peace and the highest tranquility; but where pride holds sway, there resentment, anger, disturbance, and discord confound everything without ceasing. Therefore, my brothers, beware of pride, because if it cast down the exalted angels from heaven, when would it not condemn poor cloistered men? It made demons out of angels, and without doubt it makes companions of demons out of monks. Follow humility at all times with all your strength, and flee every pride and display as much as you can, because unless you greatly humble your souls, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Walk always before the Lord Jesus in the simplicity of your heart, having a pure conscience in all things, lest your humility become brutish; for it contributes nothing to salvation to acknowledge oneself publicly as a sinner, and in

by persevering in evil, not to amend his fault. For the true servant of Christ sanctifies his humility by good works, and by continual repentance amends every guilt of his past life. Daily he calls back to memory the evil he remembers himself to have committed, and groans deeply that he has grievously offended the Lord. He walks with great caution, and so laments past sins committed that he in no way commits further things to be lamented.

The monk who is truly humble follows the Lord Jesus with a pure conscience, and fears nothing in this world more than offending the master whom he imitates. Whatever he does, and wherever he goes, he always keeps the Lord Jesus present in his thoughts, and by continual meditation examines how he may please him alone. For this is true and Christian humility, and humble Christianity: to wash away sin in true compunction, and to preserve the conscience in all purity at every time, not only through fear of punishments, but rather through love of Christ.

True humility of monks continually does whatever good it can for the honor of God, and intends to do nothing that it knows displeases Christ. True humility of monks neglects none of the things that God has commanded, and always flees as deadly the things that he has forbidden. The penitent monk, humble in the compunction of tears and serving the Lord in the fervor of charity, is the companion of the holy angels, the friend of the citizens of heaven, and very fearsome to demons. For demons fear and flee nothing more than the humility of the servants of Jesus Christ, because, since they themselves are most proud by their vicious will, they are most violently tormented by the devotion of the humble. For where true humility is, demons cannot remain; for just as ice is dissolved by fire, so malignant spirits are scattered by the presence of a humble monk.

O humility, venerable mother and guardian of all virtues, yours is the kingdom, yours the power. You bestow the kingdom on the humble; you grant the glory of eternal happiness to the meek. Without your guidance no one comes to heaven; he who follows you does not fear hell. He who gathers works of virtue without you is like one who carries dust into the wind. You are the seasoning of all good works, because just as food in the mouth of the eater is not savory without salt, so without your companionship no one is made a friend of God.

Humility made the Son of God man; humility will liken the servant of Christ to a holy angel. An angel, through pride and by his own choice, was made a devil; and a Christian man, through humility, becomes an angel. Humility opens heaven to the meek servants of God, and pride plunges arrogant men down to hell. Humility makes friends of God, and pride makes companions of demons. Humility enlightens the mind to true wisdom, and pride blinds the understanding of the one whom it has possessed. Humility purges the man whom it possesses of all disordered affections, and pride fills its worshiper with every crime and filthiness. Humility [unclear] the lover
On the True Humility of Monks

Humility makes the one who has it a servant of God; but pride makes him a slave of the devil. Humility makes a man wise in the law of the Lord; but pride renders a man foolish, away from the knowledge of the Most High. Humility brings the poor man into the fellowship of God; but pride makes the rich man members of the devil. Humility is the mother and nurse of all virtues; but pride is the source of all vices. Humility, through charity, covers a multitude of sins; but pride alone brings in the fullness of all vices.

Humility makes the good works of monks most pleasing to God; but pride renders the efforts of the arrogant idle before the Creator. Humility receives from the Lord whatever it asks; but almighty God resists the prayers of the proud. Humility always has devout confidence, with cheerfulness of mind, in the mercies of the Lord; but pride, with the sting of despair, begets disturbance in a man. Humility always has joy of spirit in the love of Christ; but destructive fear always occupies pride. Humility, the fosterer of good works, neglects none of the spiritual exercises; but pride despises all pursuits of salvation.

Humility justifies sinners; but pride condemns its followers. Humility makes a man near to God; but pride makes him alien from the grace of God. Humility diligently obeys the commandments of God with a peaceful will; but pride struggles against the precepts of the Most High. Humility heaps up the merits of everlasting happiness; but pride prepares for itself the most grievous torments of hell. Humility grants security at the moment of death; but pride brings horrible fear and calamity upon the dying man.

Humility frees the soul of its worshiper from every anguish in the dread judgment of God; but pride accuses before the Judge all the arrogant whom it has deceived in the world. Humility will place the servants of God at the Judge’s right hand; but pride will set those to be damned at his left. Humility will plead the cause of its own and prevail in judgment; but pride, utterly confounded, will hand the arrogant over to the devil. Humility will repay its friends with the reward of eternal happiness; but pride will give the torments of perpetual damnation to all the arrogant.

Humility will be crowned without end in heaven; but pride will suffer immeasurable torment with the demons forever in hell. Humility, crowned, will reign with Christ in heaven; but pride, despised, will be tormented with the devil in punishments. Humility, joyful and glorious, will sit forever at the right hand of God; but pride, sorrowful and shameful, will lie without end in the torments of hell. Then the humble will exult in glory, and all the proud will cry out in punishment through everlasting ages with exceedingly great grief.

There the humble will stand in the sight of God and of all the saints, in great gladness and everlasting exultation, receiving for the voluntary poverty of this life unfading riches; for meekness, a kingdom; for sorrow, joy; for the love of God, dominion; for contempt of the world and voluntary mortification of the flesh, heaven.

But the proud and arrogant, placed in hell, seeing such great glory of the humble whom they despised in the world, will marvel at so sudden a change of the saints. They will be troubled with horrible fear, groaning from anguish of spirit, and saying in the fury of pride: “These are the poor and humble monks, once clothed in mean garments, separated from men, abstaining from the eating of meat and from every filthiness of the flesh, whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach. We senseless men judged their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone for us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. What does pride now profit us, by which we were then puffed up and despised the humble? And what does the boasting of riches possessed in the world bring us? All things have passed away, and we, because of our stubbornness, have been counted among the demons, since we always hated humility, and we suffer immeasurable torments without end. But the humble will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and their thought is with the Most High.”

Think on these things always, my brothers, because without doubt they are going to happen in this way. Therefore take up true humility of mind; flee every sin; keep your conscience pure, so that you may deserve to obtain the rewards of eternal life. Amen.
On the True Obedience of Monks. Homily XX.

Humility of monks, if it is true and perfect, begets the whole fullness of holy virtues. But if it lacks the splendor of virtues, true humility was never in the mind. For first of all it begets true obedience, and in all things a profound subjection for the love of God. For the monk who sojourns in the flesh truly humble shows himself in all things an eager disciple of our Savior Jesus Christ; for love of him, content with every lowliness and extremity, he glories in being subject, obedient in all things to his abbot. Humble obedience for the love of Christ is a great virtue: it opens heaven to the monk and by its strength shuts hell. Obedience restores the way of paradise and reforms peace between God and man.

This, however, is the true obedience of a monk: that which is rendered to the commands of superiors not from servile fear, but from the affection of inward charity; that which, persevering unto death not through fear of punishment but through love of justice, works good in gladness of mind. There are two most beautiful wings of the mind by which the monk flies up from earth to heaven: one of them is called humility; the other is named the obedience of subjection. The monk who has not been adorned with these wings has utterly lost both the name and the merit of his dignity. Nor should he be called a monk, but a liar and most deceitful apostate, whoever lives and dwells in a monastery without the obedience of humble subjection. For a monk without obedience is a monster of the devil, and he who resists the commands of his elders will inherit the punishments of hell.

The disobedience of the first man lost from the beginning the life of eternal happiness, which the obedience of Jesus Christ repaired. For he himself was made obedient to the Father for us unto death, and by his most innocent passion restored to us the happiness we had lost. Hence humble obedience is the road to salvation, as our holy lawgiver Benedict cries out in the Rule: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive the admonition of a loving father and effectively fulfill it, that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom you had withdrawn by the sloth of disobedience.”

Obedience is the tree of eternal salvation, which grows in the garden of monastic humility. Obedience is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and the quiet tomb of one’s own will. Obedience is the merit of heavenly happiness and the one sure lesson of monastic discipline. Obedience is the extermination of pride and all arrogance, and the persecutor of all vices. Obedience conquers every malice and extinguishes all the disordered pleasure of the flesh. Obedience makes the conscience pure and clean, and preserves true humility in the mind. Obedience is the remedy of the wounded soul and the foundation of all monastic observance. Obedience is the faithful guardian of all good works and the discipline of a sincere mind. Obedience is the beginning of mortification and the glorious ornament of a monk. Obedience is the preserver of peace and concord, without which the vigor of monastic discipline perishes. Obedience always directs the keenness of the mind toward God; and he who is truly mortified in spirit despises all the customary things of this world. Obedience makes the monk near to God and far removed from all stains of the soul. Obedience is the adornment of the soul and the garment of beauty, without which no one will come to the kingdom of eternal brightness. Obedience is the mother of victory, and he who knows how to be humbly subject for the honor of God will obtain the crown of martyrdom in heaven. Obedience distinguishes the monk from the world, and he who follows it with his whole heart will be great before the Most High. Obedience is the consummation of Christian perfection; in its humble workshop, the more a monk has advanced, the holier he becomes. Obedience is sure security in the hour of death, because the monk who is about to depart from here will fly away the more securely, the more ready he has been for obedience to commands. Obedience is the rewarder of the humble and the chief sign of merits. Obedience is the rule of Christian meekness and the strongest nourishment of inward charity. Obedience is the shade of chastity and the ornament of innocent purity. Obedience is the wisdom of monks, and to acquiesce in the commands of prelates is the highest philosophy of those who live in the cloister. Obedience and humility are the riches of monks,

and riches; and to keep the memory of the Lord’s Passion continually in the mind is the greatest sweetness above all the feasts of the world. Obedience and humility make the monk; but whoever is rebellious and proud wears the monastic habit without cause.

Obedience is the voluntary mortification, alive in the mind, of the members; and the merit of its dignity is so great that a man has nothing greater to offer in honor of God. Let each person offer for the love of God what he can: beyond doubt, he has offered more than all who has slain his own will for God’s sake through obedience. It is indeed a great good to distribute one’s possessions for the love of Christ to the use of the poor, and to relieve the want of the needy with alms. But as much as the whole outweighs the part, as much as the free choice of the will is nobler than necessity, as much as heaven is distant from earth, so much more has he offered who, for the love of God, has of his own free will denied himself forever.

For whatever temporal substance you have offered to God is not yours, but another’s, and is of less value, both in estimation and in reward, than what is your own. You have one thing of your own which, when offered, pleases God above all things. What is this but free will, which the almighty Creator has placed in your power? And a good will is greater than all riches: nothing richer is offered to God, nothing more acceptable is consecrated to him.

This most precious gift, my brothers, you once offered to God when, denying yourselves and all worldly things for his honor, you put on the monastic habit. Remember, I beg you, the words of your holy profession, and let that solemn promise never depart from memory, which each one of you made in the sight of God before us, saying: “I, brother John, promise stability, conversion of my ways, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery, which has been built in honor of blessed Martin, in the presence of Dom John, abbot.”

Behold the bond by which we have voluntarily bound ourselves to obedience; behold the service we have professed. For these are the vows which our lips uttered; these are the sacrifices of devout dedication which we offered to God. Certainly, my brothers, great are the things we have promised, and the necessity laid upon us to keep what we have professed is greater still. For unless we faithfully observe everything that the rule of our holy father Benedict commands us, the almighty justice of God will judge us severely as perjurers and wicked transgressors.

For it is very dangerous not to render to God what has been promised, and through forgetfulness of the holy institution to violate one’s purpose. Therefore, having been charged with the office of pastoral care, I am accustomed daily to admonish you to the observance of regular discipline; nor henceforth will the necessary word of salvation ever be lacking to you, so long as my spirit shall remain in this prison-house of the flesh. But you, I beg you, take care that you are not fruitless hearers, since the matter concerns the soul, which once lost is never recovered.

Whoever among you have come to the monastery to run the course of intellectual combat, whoever for the love of Christ have once renounced your own will and the world, take up holy obedience as the helmet of salvation, and you will bring back a sure victory over the enemy.

For obedience is the strongest armor of monks, against which no adversities will be able to do harm. For Scripture says: “He who keeps the commandment will experience no evil.” Likewise in Proverbs it is said thus: “An obedient man will speak of victories.” Obedience makes a monk invincible in all temptations; and he who follows in all things the counsel of his superior will never suffer loss to the salvation of his soul. For obedience is a short and rough road, by which one quickly ascends to the summit of perfection.

But the monk who is a true soldier of Christ never trusts his own judgment, but in all things follows and observes the direction of his shepherd. Indeed, he who is a true lover of Christ, who wholly desires to be a faithful monk, loves his abbot as the vicar of God, and in all things always cheerfully submits, as one obedient, to his commands, counsels, and ordinances.

But so that a monk may be able to do this with confidence, no boy, no unlearned man, no carnal man, no one lacking discretion, nor one light-minded or inexperienced in spiritual combats, should be appointed abbot, but a man gray-haired in character, learned in the divine Scriptures, walking in the spirit in the true conduct of holiness, devout, gentle, tranquil in mind, and discreet, who knows how to show both judgment to the wicked and mercy to the well-disposed. For whenever an unquiet, turbulent, indiscreet, and inexperienced man is set over monks as abbot, at once the integrity of regular discipline suffers shipwreck.

Subjection and humble obedience must perish together when subjects cannot have firm confidence in their shepherd. For if the abbot is a mocker of his brothers, or a harsh despiser of the weak, who will open to him any secret of his heart? Therefore at the beginning the greatest care must be kept, that such a prelate be appointed as shepherd over destitute sheep, one who seeks nothing other than the honor of God and the salvation of souls.

The monk who has obtained such a shepherd should give thanks to God, since in these times of ours one is rarely found who knows how to show himself in all things a worthy and suitable prelate. He is deservedly to be loved by all his subjects, and honored in the monastery with continual reverence as the vicar of Christ. Let the thoughts of all be opened to him securely, since he seeks nothing other than the progress of each one. If the physician of sick bodies must be prudent, experienced, and endowed with the highest discretion, how much more fitting is it for the abbot, who is physician of souls, to be an excellent man?

Happy are the monks to whom the mercy of God has provided a useful and suitable shepherd, if indeed it has also not denied them the understanding of this very thing. Otherwise, a good shepherd is not recognized in his uprightness by bad sheep, but

because of the ingratitude of the wicked he is rather crucified with the Lord. For monks’ judgments are often blind whenever an opinion is sought about prelates; and those who by their conduct corrupt the integrity of the order rarely judge truly and rightly about pastors. Because of the ingratitude of subjects, rulers are often changed for worse ones; and monks who despise a good and useful pastor while he is present in this life have received a foolish and useless successor by the just judgment of God.

Those who are subject in simplicity walk rightly; and those who truly imitate Christ do not pass judgment on the one who presides. For we have one whom we may follow, the shepherd of faithful souls, our Lord Jesus Christ; looking faithfully to him in mind, we shall not rashly judge the visible shepherd. “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “have sat on the chair of Moses: do what they tell you, but do not imitate what they do.” Hear these things, O monk, and you who are a zealous lover of your own salvation, consider the pattern of obedience that you should follow.

The abbot bears Christ’s vicarship in the monastery; whether he is good or bad, he deserves the obedience of all his subjects not by his own merit, but in the name of Christ. For we understand the saying, “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me,” not of the apostles alone, but of any prelate in the Church of God who has been appointed guardian and ruler of souls. Therefore, if you have an abbot who is good, suitable, and holy, hear his voice as the command of one who stands in God’s place, and whatever he commands you, be obedient in all things. Let his teaching be for you the rule of living, and his holy conduct an example of purer formation. For he is a friend of God and the vicar of Jesus Christ: by the one he deserves that you love him; by the other, that you obey him in all things when he commands.

But if you have obtained a pastor who is crude, inexperienced, or certainly less suitable, beware, I beg you, of wishing rashly to examine his actions; rather think that your sins deserve to have a useless pastor. Consider him not as what he is, but as what he is called; and honor the pastor for love and reverence of him whose vicarship marks him. Remember at all times that the obedience you promised to God must be shown purely and simply to his vicar, since, if the abbot is evil in his conduct, he nevertheless does not lose the vicarship of Christ unless he is lawfully deposed. Nor does the reprobate life of your pastor release you from the obedience promised in your religious profession.

The sentence of our customary proverb is to be feared: “Reprobate monks do not deserve to have a good abbot.” Do not suppose, dearly beloved brothers, that this example has been hurled at you; for I do not trust that I am a bad pastor, though I cannot deny that I am crude and inexperienced. Nor have I ever admitted any suspicion of evil about you, since we seek nothing more than to nourish and enlarge fraternal charity in all things. Monks frequently come to us, wandering either with reason or without cause, who for the most part turn the matter of their instability back
On the true obedience of monks.

...against abbots. But I, who desire you to be instructed in everything holy and useful, exhort and admonish your charity as a father: from now on do not lend your ears to these meddlesome wanderers, who disparage the conduct of their pastors and strive to hide their own crimes by denouncing others. It is not the necessary integrity of monastic discipline to shift the blame for the rebellion and disobedience of subjects onto the head of the pastor.

The man who is a true monk does not rashly judge another’s affairs; and the man who is a son of humble obedience does not investigate pretexts for rebellion. But he who yields consent to the passions of the flesh can never be at rest; and he who scrutinizes another’s life is a despiser of his own salvation. A monk founded in the love of God does not pass judgment on the command of his elder; and he who always beholds Christ as present venerates his pastor as an angel of God. Boldness makes a monk degenerate; and presumption has hurled many into prison. A petulant, wanton, and insolent monk has lost the purpose of holiness; and unless he is brought back to his senses by harsh chastisement of the flesh, he has already set his foot toward hell.

He who, with curious rashness, weighs the command of his elder is not obedient; and he who is saddened by an order is not a true disciple of Christ. For true obedience does not murmur, does not hesitate, does not grieve, does not seek a loophole, does not delay, does not excuse itself, nor does it show the least sign of unwillingness. At the command of the elder, for the love of Christ, it always rejoices, hastens gladly, and obeys cheerfully with speed.

For what else is a monk but an unceasing combatant, who, armed with the virtues of humility and obedience, always keeps watch in the arena of struggle, and, under a threefold battle line, fights more strongly as victor against himself? Blessed is that monk who, doing violence to himself, has learned to overcome the will of the flesh, and by the continual practice of spiritual warfare climbs the steep mountain of true obedience. Truly blessed is that monk who, having despised every consolation of the world, has placed his whole self in the love of Jesus Christ, and now desires nothing further among visible things.

It is not for monks to seek riches, honors, and pleasures in this world; nor does it befit a soldier of Christ to think of anything except Christ. O monk three and four times happy, who, for the love of Christ, mortifies his own will even to the end of life, and perseveres humble in true obedience. How great a good humble obedience is before God, my brothers, no one can sufficiently declare, since divine testimony willed to prefer it to all sacrifices. It is obedience that reconciles the soul to God and, because of the shedding of blood, crowns the martyrs.

For the monk who, for God’s sake, of his own free will binds himself to the perpetual obedience of religion, if he lives rightly according to his vow, certainly bears a long martyrdom. Obedience, therefore, is martyrdom without the shedding of blood; and voluntarily to subject oneself to a man for God’s sake is a mighty torment of the flesh. The soul that [unclear] humility and...
Homily XX

Whoever truly loves obedience undoubtedly reaches the crown of martyrdom. It is an arduous work and an exceedingly laborious struggle for a free man to despise himself, and forever to surrender himself wholly, and all his own will, under the command and power of another. But let us look with faithful eyes upon the reward of this struggle, and we shall reckon all the hard and bitter things of this life as a kind of childish game, which is seen for an hour and afterwards appears nowhere. For, as the Apostle, the lover of Christ, says: the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.

The crown which martyrdom once bestowed upon the saints for Christ, humble obedience will today prepare for the true lovers of Christ. For the monk who is truly humble and obedient for Christ dies secure and without fear, as one who, faithfully serving under the command of his superior, is freed from every demand for an accounting. For he who, living at the nod of his shepherd, walks rightly in all the commandments of God, can commit nothing that may be brought before the judge. He is defended by the testimony of the abbot, under whose direction he has lived rightly and without complaint.

Consider, brothers, the law of obedience according to which you promised to live, and know that you have made necessary what had been voluntary, when you solemnly consented to the judgment of monastic tradition. It is no longer permitted you to withdraw from the holy purpose, nor can you revoke a vow once uttered. If you do all things according to the holy Gospel of Christ and the rule of Father Benedict, which you vowed, let there be no doubtful hesitation in you: you will be blessed, and you will receive from the Lord the reward owed to the saints. But if, forgetful of your promises, you violate the vow of holy purity made to God, if, despising the spiritual life, you live according to the flesh, I now declare to you from your own law that you are most certainly to be condemned by our Lord Jesus Christ, the judge of all, whom you have mocked and despised. For it is far better to promise nothing than to violate a vow.

Therefore the condition of your salvation is placed in this one thing: that, just as you once promised God, you persevere until death according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, living in all purity of mind and body. For a Christian man who has not vowed monastic conversion can be saved by living rightly according to the Gospel; but he who has once become a monk will not be saved unless he has kept until death all the things required for the monastic institution.

Listen, then, O monk, to a brief, solid, and true word. You are a monk: if you live as a monk, you will be saved; but if you live otherwise, you will not be saved, but will receive your portion among the apostate spirits, because you have mockingly despised God, to whom you lied. Now therefore call yourself back to yourself; diligently examine your conscience concerning your whole life; weigh exactly how you have fulfilled thus far the vows you promised. But

Yet let the judgment of your own self-assessment be suspect to you, unless the judgments of others also confirm you. Always remember that hour when you first entered the monastery for the sake of conversion, so that, whenever you find your soul growing sluggish from the fervor of holiness, you may renew it according to the former training of your novitiate.

You will quickly be able to become a good monk if you always and everywhere preserve obedience and humility in all things. True obedience in a monk gathers many virtues within him; humility, however, preserves those virtues once gathered, lest they flow away. Be ready at all times to obey the commands of your shepherd, and however much progress you have made in the struggle of holy combat, do not lift up your soul in any estimation of your progress. For what are our righteousnesses before the Lord? Or what good can we do that he has not given? Since God, who is sufficient to himself in all things and alone perfect, has no need of our good deeds, for he is the highest and unchangeable good, in comparison with whom all our justifications are less than nothing.

Therefore a monk placed under an abbot, in the humility of one truly obedient, walks securely; and if he perseveres to the end, fighting and conquering, he will be gloriously rewarded. Truly, brothers, the humility of your obedience delights me, which you show faithfully to the almighty Lord. In this respect I do not regard myself as your prelate, but as your companion and the humble minister of you all, though a more useless one. Therefore, in those matters that concern your salvation, I beg you, do not look at my person as I speak, but rather at the common Lord of all, for love of whom you have set me, an unworthy man, over you as abbot. For I will not be troublesome to you while you are running well; but if anyone turns aside from the way of truth, I am compelled, even unwillingly, to oppose him as far as I can.

Let a monk always remember his entrance into the monastery, and never forget the first resolve of his training. In all your works too, O monk, always remember that you are not lasting long upon the earth, but will shortly depart from this life, and that you will die perhaps when you do not expect it. Therefore keep inviolate your purpose of holiness, and always be watchful in good works, so that when the Lord comes and calls you, he may find you prepared. Remember that you are a pilgrim on earth, and have here no abiding city; but just as a traveler hastens quickly toward the end of his journey, so death approaches you daily without interruption.

Therefore, while you are healthy, set the house of your conscience in order, so that you may not fear death, since he rarely dies well who is not prepared as one who will die each day. O how securely that monk departs from this life who, keeping his conscience clean in all purity, conducts himself at all times, without reproach, according to the full integrity of the rule of our most holy lawgiver, even to death. Let your mind continually [keep before it] our Lord Jesus Christ as present, indeed as nowhere absent.

Let him keep it in memory, and let no hour pass in which you do not think with thanksgiving of him suffering for you. Stand in humility and true obedience, and no adversities will ever prevail against you. Just as a tree that sends many great roots into the earth is not easily torn from its place, so a monk who possesses charity and obedience in humility, together with the other virtues, is by no means overcome by demons. Obedience is a great virtue, brothers; it plants the other virtues in the mind, and, once planted, guards them through the ministry of humility. May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who was made obedient for us unto the death of the cross, enlighten your hearts by his grace, and sweetly inflame your minds at all times for the observance of the regular life; he who lives and reigns with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.
On Continence and True Chastity. Homily XXI.

I would greatly wish, my dearest brothers, that I had obtained from God that grace by which I might be a worthy and suitable pastor for you in deed as well as in word. For I know, and it does not escape me, how dangerous a thing the governance of souls is for a young and inexperienced man such as I am, when one who has not yet learned to direct and govern himself according to the rule of justice presumes to undertake the teaching of others. I blush to open my mouth among you to teach, since after only a short time as a disciple I am compelled, before maturity, to be a teacher. Yet since it has so pleased you, and you have wished to have me, a young man, as your master, spare me, for necessity compels me to fulfill, according to my strength, the office entrusted to me. Help me with your prayers, I beg you, brothers, so that the mercy of God may supply the strength that the inexperience of age denies.

For I desire you to walk before God in all purity of mind and body, so that you may please him to whom you gave yourselves from the beginning. Look to our Lord Jesus Christ as the guide of the journey you have undertaken toward heaven: born of the ever most chaste Virgin Mary, he preserved forever the most perfect chastity of mind and body. Follow this teacher, into whose service you have consecrated your hands, so that you may preserve continence for yourselves not only in body, but also perpetually guard in mind a chastity brighter than sapphire and carbuncle. For chastity is a most beautiful virtue, especially fitting for those in the cloister; through it every impulse of lust is curbed under the yoke of reason, and, the madness of vices being extinguished, the body’s disposition is preserved in complete honorableness.

An incontinent and wanton monk, who follows the filthy lust of the flesh, is counted with the demons who withdrew from the Lord. For there are three things without whose perpetual observance no one is to be reckoned worthy of being named among monks. The first of these is the obedience of humble and true subjection; and the second, the renunciation of everything of one’s own.
of [unclear], as the Rule commands; the third vow, perpetual continence and the inviolate custody of chastity. If a monk violates any one of these, he corrupts the purpose of his order.

Chastity is supported by two companions, namely fasting and temperance; if it is ever deprived of them, it very quickly, without doubt, begins to totter. Chastity is the greatest adornment of monks; adorned with it, they will be brought into the company of the angels. Nothing is more beautiful than chastity: it makes clean what was conceived from unclean seed, it makes a member of the household out of an enemy, and an angel out of an earthly man.

Chastity is the most beautiful virtue of all virtues; when it is promised to be kept even until death for the love of Christ, it is rewarded with an inestimable prize. Chastity is nearest to the fellowship of angels, and is the highest medicine of the Christian mind. Chastity is the beloved dwelling place of Jesus Christ, the eternal King, and the wondrous beginning of future incorruption. Chastity is the fullness of heavenly grace, through which every corruption of nature is restored. Chastity is the most powerful virtue of all, through which, in a fragile vessel, nature is conquered in a wondrous contest. Chastity imitates the angelic life, and knows no sprinkling of stain in the midst of the mire.

Blessed is the man who has truly deserved to receive from the Lord God the gift of chastity, and has kept it inviolate until death in Christian humility. He is chaste who, pure in mind and body for the love of Jesus Christ, abstains from every defilement of the flesh; who, with the fervor of the Holy Spirit, burns sweetly in the love of God; who desires absolutely nothing in this world; who always longs to be and to live with Christ.

He is chaste who, mindful of his profession in spiritual warfare, restrains the movements of the flesh by reason, and at once, from the very beginning, firmly checks all the itching sparks of lust. He is chaste who, as soon as a carnal thought has begun to strike the mind, implores divine help with tears, and does not cease from prayers until he feels that the fire of itching ardor has been utterly extinguished.

He is chaste who flees every matter and occasion of lust; who has made a covenant with his eyes that he should think nothing about a woman, and sets a guard over his senses, lest any foul or immodest things be thrust upon them. He is chaste who avoids the company of the wanton, and always turns his eyes away lest he behold vain things. He is chaste who detests the frequent company of all women, and who at all times regards his own frailty with fear and vigilance as suspect.

He indeed is chaste who in mind and body imitates the angelic nature, and who admits no corruption in holy conduct. Chastity is a gift of grace, not a work of nature or of human effort. Chastity makes a humble monk most pleasing to God, since he who lives in mortal flesh without corruption is a companion of the angels. He who has attained true chastity is always humble; and he who understands its nature does not arrogate its possession to himself, but to the Lord who gave it. For no one is chaste by his own strength, since frail man cannot conquer nature.
Homily XXI.

It is not enough unless he who created nature and all things has given it. For whenever nature is overcome by chastity, God is manifestly working together with man. Chastity itself has a difficult beginning in the young, until the movement of unlawful thought is brought into contempt. Chastity overcomes fornication by fleeing rather than fighting, because lust is girded about with so many subtle weapons that it must be avoided before it is engaged.

Therefore, whenever the soul is touched by the movements of lust, let divine help be invoked without delay. Let no time for deliberation be given to an unclean thought, but as soon as it begins to be felt, let it be brought into contempt by the remedy of forgetfulness. With a deceitful enemy, one who always uses ambushes, no conversations at all are to be mingled; and with the unclean thoughts of the flesh no counsels are to be discussed. For unless you crush the serpent’s head, it slips away; and unless you immediately repress the movements of lust from the beginning, they grow strong.

The holy apostle of Christ, Paul, warns that one must fight against every vice, but he commands that fornication alone be fled. We carry about with us the material for victory against ourselves; therefore he wills that we flee the enemy. Chastity is nourished by fasting; by gluttony it suffers shipwreck. Therefore, if you love chastity, love fasting, so that it may have its necessary nourishment.

He who is chaste follows the diligence of the bee; and he who is truly a monk, as if adorned with every flower, is adorned with all virtues. Not everyone is chaste who does not know lust, but he who, in pure and clean flesh, for the love of Christ alone, also obtains holiness of mind. Otherwise, what does the purity of the dwelling profit, if the inhabitant is foul and unclean?

Blind paganism once had its virgins sacrificing to Vesta; but because they did not offer the chastity of their bodies to the true God, nor hold right faith in their mind, they went down into the depth of hell with their demons, whom they worshiped. For he is chaste who, for love of the Creator, restrains the flesh from every lust, and offers the mind, adorned in every way with holy virtues, to God himself. Outside faith in Jesus Christ today there is no true chastity, nor any that merits eternal salvation.

Live chastely, O monk; conduct yourself pure and holy; and as long as the spirit remains in the body, do not presume to have confidence in the chastity of clay. The food of chastity is fasting and abstinence, and in every action the strengthening of wholesome continence. But when you have attained all things, do not trust in yourself, because he fell from heaven whom we know to have eaten nothing. The mortification of the body is very necessary and useful for preserving the beauty of chastity; but however much you have advanced in both, do not trust in yourself, but always keep watch, hope in the help of the Lord, and fear.

For unless you continually and most urgently keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, the house of your conscience will quickly be overthrown. He runs in vain who presumes to guard chastity by his own strength. For unless the Lord has built the dwelling of chastity, he labors in vain who builds the wall of abstinence. And unless you have become, with all your strength, a co-worker with divine grace, you will by no means obtain the beauty of chastity.

For God will not make you chaste without your will, nor will you attain this great gift unless he comes to the aid of your weakness through his mercy. Therefore, O monk, it will be yours, with a good will, to offer the desire for chastity, and with humble confidence to await sure increase from the Lord. Apply what is yours, and the Lord’s help will not be lacking. Chastity is a gift of grace, not of nature; and to live in the flesh as though beyond the flesh belongs to angelic strength, not human.

Yet it is not difficult for a man of good will to preserve chastity, especially one who is separated from the tumult of secular people and lives solitary in the midst of monks. A monk also who, young and innocent, enters a monastery of good reform, if he continually occupies his mind in the fear of the Lord, is less attacked by lust. For experience of desire is destructive, since, as someone has truly said:
Venus wants to conquer souls, not satisfy them.

But a monk zealous for his own salvation can easily extinguish the fire of lust, if, fleeing idleness and repletion, he is willing to occupy himself continually in spiritual exercise. For among all the vices, none attacks chastity more greatly or more dangerously than repletion and idleness. If a monk has overcome these two evils, he will easily guard chastity. Hence the most holy fathers of monks, wishing to cut away the causes of lust, established for us a sparing and scanty diet in fixed measure, so that the body may be sustained for necessity and not fattened for lust. They also ordained restriction of sleep as useful for monks, because immoderate rest inflames the flesh no less than gluttony. But they wished idleness, as the most destructive plague of the soul, to be far from cloistered men, most wisely dividing the time so that a monk would never be found idle.

Hear these things, brothers, and grasp them in your mind, you who carry a great treasure in a fragile little body. Flee idleness; always do some good thing, so that as often as the devil the tempter approaches, he may find you usefully occupied. For truly, he who is idle lies open to the snares of the tempter; but he who is occupied in good work has closed every entrance to snares. Therefore the mind must be occupied with continual exercise, so that it may never be found idle.

Blessed is that monk who occupies his mind at all times in good exercises, and never sleeps in the slumber of torpor and sloth. Blessed is the spiritual soldier of Christ who always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord, and immediately restrains from the beginning all the disordered movements of the flesh. For it is not enough to preserve true chastity unharmed if one plays, as though deliberating, with unclean thoughts. One must resist the first stirrings of wicked thoughts, since where delay gives rise to danger, one must immediately fight bravely. One must always keep watch against [unclear] of salvation.

our adversary [unclear], who is never overcome more quickly than if he is choked off at once from the beginning. Constant practice is needed, brothers, because a mind always occupied in holy studies is like a very high tower of strength, in which the most watchful soldier of Jesus Christ, once stationed, fears no hostile ambushes.

Therefore I beseech you, my dearest brothers, do not waste your time in idleness; do not increase within yourselves the material of vices, since you are not ignorant of the cunning of the evil spirit. Preserve continence in all things, and apply temperance, the guide of the virtues, to all your works. Always consider how you ought to walk before the Lord God in all religion and holiness, into whose words you have sworn, and live in such a way that you do not fear to appear at his judgment.

You are monks, separated from the world by voluntary promise for the service of our Lord Jesus Christ; therefore, under the necessity of salvation, you must lead a higher and holier life than the rest of your fellow Christians, and overcome every depravity of flesh and soul. For you must always be most chaste in mind and body alike, and stained by no filth of corruptible flesh. An incontinent monk is an apostate; and one who defiles his flesh with the filth of women is like one who violates an oath. Lust is a pit of hell, and despair is always very near to incontinence.

A monk who once slips into the pit of the flesh is rarely kindled to true compunction of heart. For the vice of fornication, growing strong through long habit, is not easily overcome unless it is corrected by force with contrary remedies. It is more difficult after a fall of the flesh to rise again to true chastity than to remain in continence once possessed. It is easier to fall from the state of uprightness into any vice than to correct a sin strengthened by habit. For, as a certain pagan truly says:
Easy is the descent to Avernus; but to recall the step and escape to the upper airs, this is the task, this is the labor.

Let us consider those who have fallen into this most foul pit and afterward, by the authority of their superiors, have been compelled to do penance: how do they live among the brothers? They do not have the signs of true compunction, but pass an unquiet life in dryness of heart. No devotion of mind is seen in them, but everywhere they follow the accustomed ways of the flesh. How rarely is anyone converted to the sweetness of inward love who has once plunged into the pit of fornication. For unless, before he comes into this misery, he has been grounded in the fear of the Lord, once fallen he returns with the greatest difficulty to true compunction.

Therefore live soberly, dearest brothers, and always keep watch in holy prayers, because unless you walk most cautiously in all things, you will by no means be able to escape the snares of demons. Love abstinence; guard humility above all things. For no one can suppress the impulses of his flesh who has neglected to tame gluttony and pride.

The insolent demon of fornication is never better conquered than when true humility of heart is preserved in the fullness of all virtues. For just as almighty God, resisting the proud, gives grace to the humble, so the devil, fleeing the humble, hurls the proud down into fornication. Therefore anyone who is gluttonous, eating and drinking to satiety, and desires to conquer the spirit of fornication, is carrying oil to the fire.
