For humility is the greatest virtue of monks, because they are bound to be humbler than others living their life in the world in the same measure as, by profession, they are obliged to strive and tend toward greater perfection. Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; whatever is built upon it will be overturned by no whirlwind of storm. Through

Through pride the devil fell from heaven; through humility man ascends. We are called monks in vain if we have not been humble, since, just as fire is extinguished if it lacks the fuel of wood, so a monk without humility is judged utterly unworthy of his name. By Christian humility the devil is conquered, and, as though struck by a nail, is overcome and flees. No jewel is seen more splendid than humility in the adornment of monastic life; if a monk despises it, he has denied both his profession and the humble Christ.

After humility comes prudence, which always directs all things according to the rule of reason, and does nothing except what is right, honorable, and praiseworthy. Prudence knows what it ought virtuously to seek, and it knows well what, according to the right judgment of reason, it ought to avoid. True and perfect prudence is that by which we seek that highest, unchangeable good, and order all things to their due and right end. Prudence preserves the observance of regular discipline stable in its vigor, and brings wandering monks back to the complete reform of the purpose they have lost. Prudence directs the monk on the right way of salvation, and does not allow him to turn aside in either direction. Prudence preserves peace and concord among the brothers, and orders right action in each matter.

Prudence is very necessary for you, my brothers, so that in every action you may know what you should undertake and what, in turn, you should flee. True prudence, not of the flesh but of the spirit, teaches you to despise the world and to desire only those things that are future and eternal. Prudence teaches a man to stand firm within himself, and not to turn aside from his purpose of holiness either in prosperity or in adversity. Prudence teaches him to order present things well, brings past things back to memory for instruction, and provides for the future, lest anything happen unexpectedly. Prudence corrects offenders usefully and fruitfully; all that it either does, says, or thinks, it arranges according to the judgment of reason toward its due end.

Be therefore prudent as serpents and simple as doves, because prudence without goodness is malice, and simplicity without rational prudence is called folly. For the most holy Paul, Apostle of Christ, says: The prudence of the flesh is death. Be prudent, lest you be circumvented by the deceit of others; but be simple, lest you circumvent anyone. For this is the office of the prudent man: neither to be capable of being deceived, nor to wish to deceive anyone. A prudent man does not abandon the judgment of reason, and does nothing for which he must repent. For “prudent” is so called from foreseeing.

Justice accompanies prudence, and it is the most splendid of all the virtues. For without justice all the other virtues are nothing. Justice is the preserver of religion, the mother of grace, the nurse of observance, the fosterer of truth, the begetter of peace, and the source of piety. Justice is the virtue that distributes and preserves to each person what is his own; it neglects its own advantage in order to preserve the common advantage and equity, without which no commonwealth can long subsist in peace. For he says in Ecclesiasticus:

The wise man says: A kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, injuries, insults, and various deceits. The order of justice first regards God, then one’s country, thereafter one’s parents, and afterward all people in common according to distinctions of rank and the merits of their dignities. To God, first of all, at the dictation of justice, we owe religion, faith, worship, devotion, thanksgiving, and true love from the whole heart under obedience. Next, to ourselves we owe purity of mind and body, continence with zeal for perfection, so that through obedience we may be permitted to return to him by whom we were created. In the third place, to our country we owe advantage, honor, and defense, and, as far as we can, the promotion of its welfare together with justice itself. Fourth, we are bound to show honor and obedience to our parents, and in their need care and every kind of support. Fifth, to our prelates and superiors we owe obedience and humble subjection for the love of Christ. Sixth, prelates owe teaching and nourishment to their subjects, and correction to those who do wrong. In the seventh place, we owe honor to elders and princes, and subjection without sin for the love of God. Eighth, we owe reverence to venerable persons, and honor to priests. Thereafter we are bound to offer friendship to equals, condescension to inferiors, requital to benefactors, fellowship to friends, patience to enemies, mercy to the poor, consolation to the wretched, and charity to all.

This is true justice: that we love God with the whole heart for his own sake, and our neighbor in God as ourselves, and our enemy for God’s sake, distributing to each person what is owed to him by right and providing for the benefit of all. But since excessive justice easily falls into sin, temperance is necessary for you all, and it alone makes people perfect. Temperance is a virtue that discerns by reason and conquers the movements of the soul and every lust, so that impulse in action may not exceed the equity of the law. Temperance, an excellent virtue, rules pleasures and preserves all things in due order. In all your actions, and also in your words and thoughts, apply temperance, and the discretion necessary to the virtues. Whatever good you do with discretion receives the name by merit of virtue; but what is done without discretion must be called vice. Discretion is the moderator of all virtues, and the greatest adornment of prudence and justice. Discretion is necessary not only for prelates but also for subjects, because it gives order to virtues, bestows modesty upon affections, and grants to all human counsels a most beautiful seemliness and honesty. Hence a certain wise man said:
There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits, beyond and short of which the right cannot stand.
For this, brothers, strength of soul is necessary for you, through which you may not only become steadfast in adversities, but also ready and cheerful.

in difficult matters. For who without the greatest courage of soul could despise this world with its pleasures, and persevere in holy monastic religion under the laws of obedience even until death? Courage of soul receives its strength from the love of Christ, and stands firm in the desire for virtue, no less in adversity than in prosperity. Courage walks the path of uprightness without fear, and to its enemies, by a certain holy pride, appears terrible and formidable. Courage of soul despises the injuries of the little and easily overcomes all the pleasures of the flesh. Courage lies hidden in prosperity, is shown in adversity, and is plainly manifested through patience. Strong in soul is not the man who avenges injuries inflicted on him, but the man who patiently endures them; and if he has brought his adversary into his power, he counts it vengeance enough that he could have taken revenge.

The courage of monks is to despise the world, conquer the flesh, spurn all the honors and pleasures of the world, and place all hope and confidence in God alone. The measure of courage is to be neither timid nor rash, since it advances on the straight way and declines neither to the right nor to the left. That monk is to be judged courageous who is temperate in all things, moderate, and just. Hence the most holy Pope Gregory says: The strength of the just is to conquer the flesh, to resist their own pleasures, to extinguish delight in the present life, to love the hardships of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, to despise the allurements of prosperity, and to overcome in the heart the fear of adversity. They became strong in battle, because they tame the flesh, shine with virtues, strengthen the spirit, despise earthly things, seek heavenly things; they can be killed, but they cannot be bent; nor do they, through weakness, fear to endure falsehoods, nor, when injured, are they ever silent about the truth.

Therefore the monk who is strong with true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears without judgment. For courage together with constancy is the royal road; from it the rash and obstinate man declines to the right, but the fearful, fainthearted, and timid man to the left. The monk constant and strong in soul never falls away from his purpose of holiness, but is neither crushed by adversities nor lifted up by prosperity. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: The fool is changed like the moon; but the wise man is not broken by fear, not changed by power, not puffed up by prosperity, not sunk by sorrows. For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and courage of soul. Therefore the wise man is always the same in soul; he is neither diminished nor increased by changes of circumstances, nor, like a little child, does he waver, so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

Finally, my dearly beloved brothers, perseverance is necessary for you in every good and virtuous work; without it no one ever reaches the crown of glory. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: He who perseveres to the end will be saved. Take away perseverance, and virtue will have no reward, obedience no recompense, nor does [unclear] merit grace.
That monks must live cautiously.

For perseverance alone in good works deserves to receive the crown of praise; without it, it profits nothing to have begun well. Virtue has no merit where perseverance has not given increase. The kingdom of eternal blessedness is promised not to those beginning good, but to those persevering in good until death; for not in the morning, not at midday, but when evening had come, the denarius will be paid to those laboring in the vineyard. For it is not the one who began well who is to be praised, but the one who continued well to the end who is to be honored.

Therefore, my brothers, I am accustomed earnestly to admonish you, and I must never cease, that you attentively consider your calling and walk cautiously in all religion and holiness, as befits sworn soldiers of Christ. For now is the time for doing good, because when the hour of death arrives, it will utterly cut off every ability to work. And so, as long as you live sound and unharmed, do good; always think of the future recompense, and daily grow in spiritual progress. Seek the Lord while he can be found. Let the life of Christ the Savior be your imitation; by the very foundation of your institution you are bound to follow him according to your strength, not by the steps of your feet, but by likeness of affections.

Walk cautiously in all things; always place the fear of God in true humility before the sight of your mind. For you need great purity, you who have consented in mind and body to the holy warfare of Christ. It now belongs to you, brothers, for God’s sake to despise the world and all things that are in the world with perpetual courage, to overcome every movement of carnal pleasures, to flee sin, and to occupy yourselves continually in good and holy works. Your life also, as far as human weakness allows, must imitate angelic purity and flee and detest every perversity. The holy angels are never idle, but are always intent upon the praises of God without weariness or tedium. The holy angels love God above all things, and do not withdraw from his charity even for a moment.

In imitation of them, the monk must be constant in the service of Christ and always occupied in good works according to the Gospel and the rule. The monk must have a most fervent charity toward God, and a true, ordered, and sincere love of neighbor. For fervent love for God perfects the monk and does not allow him to be idle. For the most holy Pope Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle.” For it does great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it was never true love of God. For if the foolish poet spoke truly concerning carnal love, “Let the man who does not wish to become idle love,” how much more powerfully does the most chaste love of God drive the mind it possesses toward difficult things.

Love God, brothers, with your whole heart, as far as the strength of desire can extend itself, and you will be able most easily to observe all the things that have been prescribed for you. For nothing is difficult to one who loves; rather, fervent love makes all hard things, all heavy things, and all difficult things very easy.
Sermon II.
What the good ordering of monastic life is. Sermon II.

We have said that the institution of our most holy father Benedict, which by the usual term we call a religion or order, shone forth as most holy at the beginning of its foundation, and was spread very widely and in many ways throughout the whole Church of the Latins. Hence, for very many years in this same order there shone many wise, learned, and most holy men, who magnificently illuminated the whole Church. For there are those who write that from this monastic religion of ours fifteen thousand six hundred men and nuns have been enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. This multitude of saints in the order is set before us, brothers, for imitation, not for empty boasting. What can their multitude contribute to our salvation if we do not imitate the manner of life by which they went before us?

Whenever we desire usefully to praise the most holy men of our order, let us hasten by holy conduct to come into their fellowship. For then we shall glory fruitfully in the multitude of the saints of our order, if, by living rightly, we strive diligently to increase their number. For this reason we set before you so great a multitude of saints: so that, when you see that many before you in this same order conquered the world and the flesh, you may at last rise up from your lukewarm way of life. The virtue which God’s mercy bestowed on them he will not deny to you if you ask in true charity.

They conquered the world because they loved Christ with complete devotion, despising all things for love of him. They despised all things, and the Lord Jesus provided for them whatever seemed necessary for the sustaining of life. This fervor of devotion among the monks endured for many years after the first institution of the order in great constancy, and converted the souls of many thousands of men to the Lord. But nothing among human things is stable, nothing among perishable things is lasting. Holy religion bestowed riches on the monks, until in time the daughter suffocated her mother. For, as Scripture says, all who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil.

The beloved grew fat and kicked back: made fat and enlarged with earthly possessions, he abandoned the holy pursuits of the first institution and went after vanities and false insanities; the abundance of temporal things made him poor and miserable in spiritual riches. This lamentable deformity of our order began about two hundred years after the passing of the holy father Benedict, and grew more and more with time, until at last the harmful poison spread through the whole order. Yet this deformity did not seize the order suddenly, but over the course of many years at last occupied almost the whole of it; although almighty God never wholly deprived it of good men, but always left for himself some who had by no means bent their knees before Baal. For men of mercy arose,
What is the good ordering of monastic life.

Their righteous deeds will never be delivered to oblivion: they had compassion on the ruin of the order, put their shoulder under the burden, and, with the Lord granting his aid, restored it in many places. Indeed, many different particular reforms in the order flourished many times at various periods; but there was never any general one that brought the whole order back to the integrity of regular observance. Finally, we see that the particular restorations, which we have said were many, have almost all collapsed again.

Most recently, however, in the year of the Christians 1420, when the general council was being held at Constance, a certain new and, up to now, last particular reform took its beginning in Germany. It takes the name by which it is called from a certain monastery in the regions of Saxony, then the poorest of all, which is called Bursfeld. The first author and chief of this most holy reform was John Rode, abbot of the distinguished monastery of St. Matthias near Trier. Having been appointed general visitor of the order by the aforesaid Council of Constance, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be judged reprobate, he first displayed reform in himself. For he reformed both himself first of all and the monks of the said monastery; he issued constitutions in conformity with the Rule, and obtained confirmation of the holy work from the apostolic see.

Among all the monasteries of the order, the humble and rather poor monastery of Bursfeld first received this reform, which afterward it extended to Reinhausen and to a few monasteries of Saxony near it. At length, when John Rode, abbot of St. Matthias and chief of our reform, had died, and no suitable successor for extending the undertaking that had been begun could be found in that place, John of Hagem, abbot of Bursfeld, who had already reformed certain monasteries, a holy man and very zealous for the order, was elected at the urging of Jacob, archbishop of Trier. Content with his poverty, he did not agree to leave Bursfeld, lest he should seem to have preferred riches to poverty. He therefore remained in his own monastery and was appointed over others in the place of the first reformer. Since he seemed comparable to his predecessor neither in learning nor in zeal, he was able to accomplish little for the continuation of the undertaking begun, nor could he enlarge the reform among many.

Meanwhile it happened that Nicholas of Cusa, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate of the apostolic see, came into Germany. Since he burned with great zeal for our order, he established and granted many things for its reform. Hearing of the good reputation of the aforesaid abbot at Bursfeld and of his most fervent purpose for regular discipline, he summoned him to himself, appointed him general reformer of the order, and through his industry reformed several monasteries. On this occasion, however, he instituted an annual chapter for the preservation of the reform, transferred the presidency from St. Matthias to Bursfeld, and had all things confirmed which had been done for...
Sermon II.

...he had established for the good of the reform, he obtained through the Apostolic See. The first abbot of Bursfeld in the reform was appointed John Monk of Reinhausen; the second was the John of Hagen already mentioned; the third was Theodoric, whom we have seen; and the fourth is John, who has now recently been appointed to govern.

We have therefore, dearly beloved brothers, briefly touched upon the origin of our reform, so that you may know with how much labor it began, and may persevere constant unto death in holy regular observance. For among all the reforms of our order that have preceded it, there has never been one more conformable and agreeable to the Rule of the blessed father Benedict, nor more alien from foreign inventions. We have read the statutes of almost all the other reforms, but we judge none more agreeable than ours to the Rule according to the purity of Benedict’s intention. This is the most holy Bursfeld reform in the order, which both teaches true obedience and preserves subjection in humility. In this holy religious life there live monks who are poor and without private property; they live humble, they live obedient, they live chaste.

O venerable union of monks, in which doubled charity commands, obedience serves as a soldier, humility complies, prayer keeps watch, perseverance fights, holy chastity triumphs. This is the school of regular discipline, the teacher of Christian humility, which directs conduct toward uprightness and restrains the vices of the flesh. In this arena of virtues no one is permitted to follow his own will against the Rule; no one is forbidden to do good. In this holy union life is lived according to the purity of the Rule, and if anyone begins to stray from the path of uprightness, he is soon recalled by the diligence of the elders to the observance of justice. The Rule of the most holy father Benedict is read publicly three times a year, so that no one may try to excuse himself from observance under the guise of ignorance.

There are two things that promise me great hope for the perseverance of this holy reform: namely, the annual chapter and the careful visitation of the monks every two years. If either of these is omitted at any time, the reform is at once endangered. Therefore consider now, dearly beloved brothers, and take the utmost care, as far as you can, that you do not uselessly occupy this monastery of the blessed bishop Martin under the title of so venerable a reform; for unless you live according to the Rule and the statutes of the order, purely, holily, and blamelessly, you trust in the name of God in vain.

We shall give you a few admonitions for your salvation; by the zealous observance of them you will deservedly possess both the name and the dignity of our Bursfeld reform. First of all, direct your striving with all your desires toward monastic perfection; and whenever you feel it growing lukewarm, renew it at once by attentive remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and most innocent death. For even if we are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, nevertheless we are bound to strive for perfection with all our desires. For as soon as a monk casts aside the effort to make progress, he falls into the pit of falling away.
The memory of the Lord’s Passion, with thanksgiving, to be made daily.
What the ordering of a good monastic life should be.

According to what the holy custom of our reformation has established for you to observe, firmly preserve your effort to make progress in the desire you have conceived. Therefore in the morning, when you are awakened and rise for Prime, do these things in secret. Examine and consider the course of the coming day that lies before you, and prudently think about what useful thing is at hand to be done. Set before yourselves in your hearts how carefully you wish to live the whole day, and arm your minds with patience against all things that may happen adversely. Whatever you do, complete it in the fervor of charity, and always order all words and deeds to the praise of God.

Third, we judge it useful and necessary for you always to strive to implore divine help in all things through most devout prayers. And it seems very fitting to us, as we have often said and always admonish, that each of you at least once a day should commemorate the Lord’s Passion and, for the many benefits received from God, should say an act of thanksgiving even once. So that this may be done uniformly by each one of you, listen to this brief form which we have arranged, and, if you wish, copy it out for yourselves.

I adore, praise, bless, and glorify you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, Savior and giver of life to all faithful souls, and I give you thanks from the depths of my heart for your most holy Incarnation and your Nativity from the most pure Virgin Mary, for your Circumcision, for your flight into Egypt, for your seven-year exile there, and for your later return to the land of your temporal Nativity.

I give you thanks, sweetest Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for all your labors, journeys, and weariness, for hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, poverty, and want, and for the necessities, injuries, insults, mockeries, and slanders which throughout your whole life you endured for us willingly, not under compulsion. And as often as you moved your hand to work, your foot to walk, or as often as you opened your mouth to speak, so often I bless, praise, glorify, and humbly adore you, and with all the strength of my heart I always give you thanks, mediator of God and men, sweetest Jesus Christ.

I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful King of Heaven, for your most holy teaching, for the evangelical institution of your faith and sacraments, for the calling of the nations, for the justification of sinners, and for all your wonders and powers, and for all your benefits, which you have bestowed either on me particularly or on all others together with me generally.

I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, most kindly Savior, for your charity which you had toward the human race, and for your whole most bitter Passion and all the sorrows which you endured for us wretched people. I give you thanks, Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for the grief and sorrow of your most innocent heart, which you endured for us when the time of your impending Passion was near, when you said to your disciples who followed you: My soul is sorrowful even unto death.
Sermon II.

I ask you, by this sorrow of your heart, O Lord God: have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death, and take from me all melancholy and disordered grief, granting me at all times a saving sorrow for my sins. I give you thanks for the sadness of your most holy heart, when, placed in agony, you prayed to the Father even a third time that he would remove from you the chalice of the Passion, and, having poured forth a wondrous sweat because of your anguish, you resigned yourself wholly to his will for our sake.

I give you thanks, O King of heaven and earth, for your captivity, for the insults, wrongs, and mockeries that you endured throughout the whole time of your Passion for our salvation and that of all. I give you thanks, O Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you, bound to the column for the harsh scourging of your most tender body, for the shedding of your most holy blood, and for the immeasurable pain of your wounds. I adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns, and I give you thanks for the piercings and pains of your most holy head, for the blows, spittings, and all the mockeries cruelly inflicted by the impious upon your Majesty.

I adore you, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, carrying the most heavy weight of your cross. I adore you, stripped of your garments before the multitude. I adore you, stretched out by your hands and feet with iron nails upon the cross, and most cruelly fastened to it. I adore you, Jesus Christ, eternal King, hanging and dying for me upon the cross; and I give thanks for the pains of your wounds. I give thanks for the shedding of your most precious blood; I give thanks for your most innocent death, which you willingly endured for our sins and the sins of the whole world.

I give thanks to your boundless goodness, because you called me to your faith, because you caused me to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, and because you deigned to call me from the vanity of the world to serve you, in true tranquility of mind, in this holy congregation. I ask you by your most holy name, O sweetest Jesus, mediator between God and men; I ask you by the pain of your wounds and by the merit of your most bitter Passion; I ask you by the shedding of your most holy blood and by the power of your most innocent death: grant me forgiveness of all my sins, pour into my heart the sweetness of your most fervent love, give me perseverance with growth in all virtues, and have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death, guarding me today and at all times in your mercy, loving Jesus, from every sin and danger of mind and body, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Which of you, brothers, cannot say this brief prayer, or one like it if he has a better, once each day? For it is not lengthy, nor wrapped in foreign expressions, but brief and plain, embracing the life and Passion of Christ in a concise summary. A Christian man is exceedingly ungrateful to God, and especially a cloistered man, if he does not at least once a day make remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, devoutly rendering acts of thanksgiving. But if this prayer is too long for any of you, in the eighth homily of our exhortations we recently gave you a shorter one, to which one who finds this tedious may have recourse.

Above all, I beg you, take care that you are never ungrateful for such great benefits of God. Let this thanksgiving be made after matins, because that is a very suitable time for prayer, and the silence of the night’s rest is accustomed to increase devotion. For I say what those who have experienced it bear witness to as true: there are no prayers more effective for obtaining what is sought than those that are offered to God the Father with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and with gratitude.

The fourth thing which we have judged necessary for you for regular observance is that you keep watch in guarding the outward senses, because no one can adequately guard the city of his heart who neglects to close its gates. Love silence, and flee every tumult of this age. Apply holy prudence in all that you do, and love the secrecy of quiet. For the monk who loves public and wandering excursions has never been a true lover of observance.

Fifth, we admonish you to flee destructive idleness of the soul, since this pestilential poison nourishes the gravest vices and always gives birth to impure thoughts. Therefore whoever is a lover of virtues and loves his own salvation, whoever wishes to arrive at eternal happiness, should flee idleness as from the face of the devil, if he desires to avoid sin.

Sixth, for the purity of regular observance it is required by the necessity of salvation that the renunciation of ownership be kept inviolate by all until death. For a monk who has private property prepares for himself a road to hell. But the one who receives money and spends it in the monastery should be a public minister; no private person dares presume to do this. The possession of riches does not befit monks, who are commanded to imitate the Lord Jesus in poverty of spirit. Let us hear the holy Apostle of Christ saying: Having food and clothing, let us be content with these. By God’s mercy we provide you with necessities, not as much as the desire of disordered pleasure demands, but as much as nature, content with little, requires. And so, just as it is not lawful for you to have anything without the consent of the abbot, so, since we supply everything, it is not necessary either.

The seventh thing that makes a monk is humble obedience to superiors. For he cannot be a true monk who despises obedience and denies to his superiors the humble subjection that he promised. This disease of disobedience arises from arrogance and pride of mind, just as pus is produced from an evil ulcer. But what does Scripture say? Pride is hateful before God and men, and is the beginning of every transgression. The warfare of monks is the imitation of Christ, who obeyed the Father even unto death.

The eighth place is adorned by the most beautiful virtue, chastity; if this is despised, it is now inevitable that all integrity of the Rule collapses. For a monk is commanded, by the necessity of his salvation, to live chastely until death, and from

perpetual abstinence from all venereal pollution. For these are the three principal vows of monastic life, and to live contrary to their observance is the certain damnation of monks. For the profession of monks, under sentence of eternal damnation, commands them to live without property, under obedience to their shepherd, and in perpetual chastity. If one of these three is taken away, the integrity of monastic life has been violated, and transgression condemns the one who despises it.

In the ninth place, therefore, we admonish every person dedicated to God always to beware of his own will as of a venomous serpent, since unless he keeps it suspect at all times, he easily falls into the pit of damnation. Consider the Rule, which permits monks power neither over their body nor over their own will. No one sins unwillingly. If you have perfectly submitted your will in all things to God and to your abbot, you will easily avoid sin.

Tenth, what can preserve in you, my dearest brothers, the integrity of regular observance is that in all adversities and oppositions you have the most steadfast patience for the love of God. For patience is a great virtue, which by another name we call tolerance; without it no one will emerge victorious over his temptations. Therefore the Lord said in the holy Gospel: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.” What is patience, if not to bear calmly, for reverence and love of God, both one’s own injuries and those of one’s people, and all other adversities whatever? Believe me, brothers, I speak the apostle’s sentence: patience is very necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. Let the Lord Jesus be for you the living example of patience; follow him with all your strength.

Eleventh, my brothers, beware lest your hearts be weighed down with crapula, because a monk ought not eat and drink to satiety, but through love of abstinence always to stop with a certain appetite and hunger. For the wise man says: “He who loves feasts will be in want, and he who loves wine and rich foods will not become rich.” Love fasting; cherish abstinence; preserve continence and frugality in all things. These are the arms of cloistered men; these are the standards of the spiritual warfare of monks, without which the flesh is not conquered, nor are demons overcome. Abundance of foods is accompanied by useless talk; and a belly filled with wine stirs up unclean suggestions of flesh and lust. If you wish to be chaste, be abstemious. It is most disgraceful for a monk to serve his belly and his gullet, when for the love of God he has renounced all the pleasures of the world together.

The twelfth thing that makes a monk useful and vigorous in regular observance is that he be most diligent in the service of the divine. For truly, he who is a true servant of God, as all monks ought to be, is always fervent and diligent in the work of his Creator; and because he truly knows that God is present everywhere, he prepares himself with complete devotion for obedient service to him. For it is written: “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently.” Therefore, approaching...

Sing sweetly, wisely, fervently, and cheerfully in the service of the highest and unchangeable God, dearest brothers; and with all the devotion and purity of mind you can, diligently praise your creator and savior. Let all sloth be far from the hearts of those who sing psalms; let no drowsiness be admitted while praising, since, when God is present in the midst of those who sing psalms, it is altogether fitting that fervor of devout souls be present. During the time of divine service let all things be clean, all things pure, all things most full of the fervor of charity, so that wicked thoughts may have no place and all things may be done as they ought.

When the day is finished and Compline has been sung according to custom, as soon as the monk has reached the privacy of his cell, let him examine his conscience, considering with what business he has occupied himself. This is the custom of the brothers of the Bursfeld reform, excellent and praiseworthy: that no one should presume to lay himself down on his bed after Compline unless he has first taken the greatest care to examine his conscience concerning the faults or negligences committed during the day. But if, after examination, you find that during the day you have offended in anything, you know, taught by long custom, what must be done. Hidden faults must at once on the next day be wiped away by contrition and humble confession; manifest faults, however, must be brought to the chapter of faults, which is held daily. This is the custom of the reformed order; this is the institution of holy reform: that we never allow the faults of offending brothers to grow, but as soon as they begin to arise, we take care to cut them off. The soul must be cleansed daily; the purpose of holiness must be renewed daily; because, just as we cannot remain in the same state without change, so it is necessary for us, by continual exercise, to rouse the mind more frequently to its former fervor of charity.
What are the signs of true humility. Sermon III.

Let none of you, most beloved brothers, deceive himself by his own estimation of himself; let no one seduce his heart by foolish and empty presumption. Not all who desire to seem humble are humble before God; nor are those who keep silence under injuries always truly patient. For the roots of true virtues lie hidden in the secrecy of the heart, and not in the mere outward display of presentation. We see certain men among you who desire rather to be regarded as humble than truly to be so, and who show many signs of pride, but either no signs of humility, or certainly very few. We have deep compassion, as indeed we ought, for those who err so greatly, who desire to have the name of virtue but despise virtue itself. Whom, I ask, do you deceive, wretched men? Do you not shamefully destroy yourselves by misleading yourselves, who, despising truth, love falsehood?

So that you may know how proudly you live, we shall set forth in order the marks and signs of true humility; some of these remain hidden in the heart alone, while others, breaking forth outwardly also,
Let this be for the monk a true mirror of perfect humility, in which, looking each day, he may examine himself.

The first mark of true humility, then, each person can recognize in himself when he is able to regard himself as lower and more worthless than all people, not with painted speech, but by the humble judgment of the heart. This is the greatest sign of deep humility: that a monk, always advancing toward a better way of life, should believe himself to be a useless and unworthy servant of God. True humility belongs to the heart, not to speech; it is the pursuit of the mind, not merely of bodily display. That monk is truly humble who loves God above all things, who always keeps himself pure in every respect from every transgression of God’s commandments and of the rule, who does great works of devotion and justice, and who, by a true estimate of himself within himself, thinks lowly things of himself.

The second mark of true and deep humility is attained by the one who, running well in the fear of the Lord and persevering, at all times confesses his negligences before God and men. For the more he has advanced in good works, the more he sets his sins and negligences before the eyes of his mind. He carries continual contrition in his heart for his offenses; and always pierced in spirit, praying and groaning, he asks the Lord with tears for pardon and mercy. Nor does he pray only for his own sins, but also for the sins of the whole world. The memory of one’s own offenses is the greatest remedy against the lifting up of the mind.

The third mark of humility is that he desires to keep in secret with himself all the good works he does, and, out of zeal for humility, hides his progress. For the humble man does not boast vainly, nor does he seek praise from men, who hopes for the glory of eternal blessedness. Whoever among you thinks himself humble and a true monk, let him not despise this sign of deep submission and abasement for God’s sake.

The fourth mark of true humility is that, willingly descending into the abyss of contempt for himself, he regards all his brothers as better than himself before God, even those who are openly sinning; forgetful of his good deeds, he wisely considers his own evils; but passing over others’ evils in silence, he reveals at the proper time the good things they have done. This is the condition of true humility: always to admire and proclaim the good works of others, and to make little of his own and prudently hide them for the avoidance of pride.

The fifth sign of true humility is that, having attained it, he is quiet in his simplicity, and does not speak of others’ defects unless compelled either by reason of office or by the command of charity. Yet in correction the humility of a prudent man preserves moderation, so that the one whom he cannot make better by rebuking more severely, he strives to admonish gently and meekly. At times he also wisely passes over rebukes, and waits for and watches for a more fitting time.
The sixth sign of humility is shown when a monk, for reproving and [unclear].
What the signs of true humility are.

In reproving the sins of others, he is slow out of love for humility, and is not found quick to do so. For one who is truly humble always considers his own weakness, and silently weighs in secret how many evils he himself has committed against God’s justice. Hence he greatly fears to reprove the deeds of others, because he recognizes himself as a sinner and therefore unworthy to judge others. We except the prelates and rulers of monks from this rule of humility only insofar as we know them to be obliged to correct their subjects.

The seventh sign of true humility is that he gladly accepts corrections and amendments for his faults and negligences, and is not embittered by any resentment against the one who reproves him. Whenever the humble man is corrected by someone, he rejoices in spirit with the Prophet, saying: “Let the just man correct me in mercy, and let him rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.” But of the proud Scripture says: “They hated the one who reproved them in the gate.” He who is truly humble loves the one who corrects him, but flees the flatterer.

The eighth sign of true humility is shown clearly when, after being corrected, he does not defend the fault, does not deny it, does not palliate it, does not excuse it, but confesses it with simple shame. A truly humble monk, when he is corrected, does not murmur, does not complain that the measure of fairness has been exceeded; but at once, falling to the ground before the judge, he cries out most meekly: “I have sinned; I confess the fault; I beg pardon; I promise amendment.”

The ninth sign of monastic humility makes the one who has it gentle, sweet, and modest in speech, and not loud in voice. A monk whom you see loud and hasty in speaking you will judge not humble, but proud and darkened. The humble man speaks modestly and almost under silence, and is always found readier to listen than to speak before others. It is shameful for a monk to raise his voice too much when he speaks, since one crucified to the world is commanded to love silence.

The tenth sign of perfect humility is possessed by the man who is accustomed to interpret in the better sense everything whatever he has heard about his neighbor. For our Savior says in the Holy Gospel: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged.” And again: “With whatever measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you.” The holy Apostle also says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts.” “Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls, not to you.”

The eleventh sign of holy humility is that he despises no man in his heart on account of any transgressions whatever, but places all before himself by merit of holiness. He even thinks that all who sin publicly are better than he, and therefore condemns no one. What evil he himself has done he always considers with himself in his heart; but he humbly weighs the good deeds of others as outweighing his own. Therefore he spurns no one, disparages no one, contemns no one, who [unclear] saved.

The twelfth perfect sign of true humility is that he does not desire to be praised by men; rather, whenever he is commended by another, he blushes, groaning with sorrow of mind. But when he hears the praises of others recited in the assembly, he rejoices in his neighbor’s praises and grows cheerful with exultant spirit. One who is perfectly humble cannot hear his own praises without bitterness of heart, because one who has placed his hope in the Lord Jesus despises all the glory of this life.

The thirteenth sign of true humility is not only to despise praises and favors in the truth of one’s mind, but also prudently to avoid those by whom one sees oneself being praised. Those who are truly humble flee their praisers; and whenever they are praised, they fall silent and answer nothing. The estimation of a great reputation is burdensome to the humble man, and the more he is proclaimed by men, the more he is confounded within himself. For true humility, when blamed, casts off the blame; when praised, it runs into danger.

The fourteenth perfect sign of monastic humility is that in corrections and detractions, if he suffers any, he conceives spiritual joy and a great increase of divine love. When injured, he is pierced with compunction and is stirred all the more to contempt of the world. Whenever he is wrongfully reproved by another, if he is humble, he judges that he has been justly corrected. For he does not consider his own innocence in the accusation, but humbly and contritely weighs how gravely he has offended God in other matters.

The fifteenth sign of perfect humility is that he never kicks back against the one correcting him, but preserves silence in all tranquility of spirit. He does not throw even the best-known faults of his reprover in his face, nor does he seek other grounds for argument. He does not complain that an insult is being done to him; he offers no excuse against the rash man; nor is he accustomed to repay words with words, but remains silent in everything as though mute.

The sixteenth sign of deep humility is that he despises all the consolations of the world and seeks no friendships among mortals. For true humility, undertaken for the love of Christ, takes delight nowhere except in Christ alone. No one can abide in the love of Christ unless he has learned to deny both his own will and the world with all its disordered pleasures. For thus the Lord says in the holy Gospel: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul besides, he cannot be my disciple.

The seventeenth sign of humility is that he does not divide himself among many things, does not greatly seek men’s support and benefits, but remains humbly in his own moderate condition, or even in extremity. For benefits received from men he is not accustomed to applaud much, but shows himself grateful with few and simple words. The little gifts of the weak dissolve spirits, and often render the unwary useless in speech [unclear].
What the signs of true humility are.
[unclear], and superfluous. Indeed, he who is truly humble takes no delight in worldly conversations, because they often hinder the purpose of purity. The love of Christ does not love publicity.

The eighteenth sign of humility: he compassionates from the heart with all who suffer for Christ’s love, and most patiently bears the faults and weaknesses of others, and prays for the correction of offenders. For true humility shows the bowels of pity and compassion toward weak sinners; but false and feigned humility, because it is truly pride, swells up against the frail with harsh and indiscreet severity, and becomes a cause of danger to many when, in correcting, it exceeds the rule of God’s charity. But he who is truly humble always fears to exceed the due measure of correction, and therefore inclines more toward mercy than toward excessive severity.

The nineteenth sign of true humility: it keeps the mind from all envy, and favors and prays for all people. It envies no one the gifts of divine goodness; it desires the grace of God for all, and rejoices in the progress of others. It judges no one unworthy of God’s benefits; it considers all better than itself. It regards the advantage of neighbors as its own, because it loves all as itself.

The twentieth sign of perfect humility: with bitterness of heart it recalls to memory the multitude of its sins, and for that reason considers itself unworthy of every benefit and grace of God. Hence, seeking the depth of humility, it imitates the publican of the Gospel, who, having the memory of his sins, did not wish even to lift his eyes to heaven. For the monk who is truly humble for Christ’s love always bears in his heart the sorrow of holy compunction and repentance for the evils he has done.

The twenty-first sign of cenobitic humility: he trusts the judgment of others more than his own, and for Christ’s sake wholly subjects his own will to another’s command. Let those among you who follow the judgment of their own head consider whether they can, or wish to, grasp this sign of monastic humility. For today we see few observers of true monastic humility, though many monks seem to be advancing in it. O times, O morals: in which we all promise humility, and very few of us truly take care to keep what we have promised inviolate.

The twenty-second sign of cenobitic humility: he abominates and despises beautiful, new, costly garments, and desires to have and wear all clothing cast off by others. He willingly uses cheaper things, and takes great delight in those things which others despise. Beautiful and ornately arranged garments do not befit a monk, but the meanest ones, by which the body may merely be defended from the injury of intemperate weather. For every curiosity is forbidden to cloistered men, who by reason of the profession they have made before God are bound to contempt of the world. Humility flees high things; it seeks what is lowly.
The twenty-third sign of monastic humility shows the monk to be servile toward the brothers, and [unclear].
Sermon III.

willingly devoted to service, and ready for whatever he shall have been ordered to do. For true humility obeys even inferiors with a most ready will, and is never indignant against the one who gives an order. As far as he can, he who faithfully loves God with his whole heart desires to serve everyone for the love of Christ. For whatever service he has given to the brothers, he firmly believes it has all been shown to Christ.

The twenty-fourth sign of humility a monk truly attains when, for the love of God, he delights in taking care of the baser tasks in the monastery, which the others despise. We read that many once climbed this step of true humility, and we do not doubt that they are of great merit before God. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The humble monk imitates Christ; the proud one imitates the devil.

The twenty-fifth sign of monastic humility is, in any gathering of people, always to seek the lowest place, and not to put oneself before either an equal or an inferior. It is not for monks to contend proudly over preeminence of place; nor is it fitting for a soldier of Christ to wish to surpass others in honor. For the true monk, who loves humility, content with every lowest position, desires to excel no one.

The twenty-sixth mark of humility most of all befits him who, though he is learned and educated, hides all learning and knowledge because of his lowly self-abasement. For the monk who is truly humble is always found readier to listen than to speak. For the divine priest Jerome says: The monk has the office not of one who teaches, but of one who mourns: he should either bewail himself or the world, and in fear await the coming of the Lord. The arrogance of monks is hateful both to God and to men, and is always liable to sin.

The twenty-seventh sign of humility is perfectly attained by him who, out of love for regular discipline, delights more in being silent than in speaking. The humble lover of Christ loves silence, and, lest he offend in speech, is accustomed to say very little. Humility is rarely found among the talkative, and he who is quick to speak casts down his own soul. A talkative and chattering monk is not without pride, and he who is foolish multiplies words. Whoever desires in spiritual combat to overcome his adversary through humility should not fail to restrain his tongue from much speaking and from every idle word. It is written in the book of Proverbs that in much speaking sin will not be lacking.

Whoever has attained the twenty-eighth sign of perfect humility will avoid laughter and all the disordered gestures of those who guffaw. Mourning chiefly befits a monk, not laughter, since he is one who has died to all the frivolities of the world. And the wise man says: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the wise man will scarcely laugh quietly.
The twenty-ninth mark of perfect humility takes its beginning from the fear of the Lord,

for whose honor, as far as he is able, he flees and detests every sin. For everyone who does not fear to sin has not truly been humble. But the monk who, according to his strength, follows Christ in true humility is accustomed to flee every sin and, as much as he can, to exercise himself in the pursuit of virtues. Humility confesses its sin, and whenever it offends even in the smallest matters, it does not rest until it has amended everything through true penitence. Whoever is truly humble is always found zealous to preserve the purity of his conscience. For charity is the nourishment of humility, and it does not allow the one who has it to be prying.

The thirtieth sign of true humility shows a monk confirmed in the purpose of holiness, and makes him subject to all the brothers, even the younger ones. Whatever his superior commands, he obeys simply, and he never debates the commands of his elder; he does not ask the reason why he orders it so. If impossible things are commanded, he is ready in spirit; for whatever is hard and arduous, he is prepared without contradiction. He is directed by the counsel of his superior; he believes him, trusts him, obeys him; he is willingly governed by his command.

You have now heard, my dearly beloved brothers, the thirty marks of true humility. O good God, where are the works? Which of us will boast that he has true humility, so that he suffers no defect in these signs? These, shame to say, are our times, in which the charity of many has grown cold, the integrity of holy religion is perishing, and the devotion of almost all has breathed its last. Our monks seek holiness without the merit of virtues; they wish to have merit without the exercise of labor; therefore today no saint is found in the monastery. The fervor of holy compunction in many is either very rare or lukewarm, because where one lives for flesh and blood, the fervor of inward charity is not possessed.

It is not enough for you, O monk, who boast of observance, to have nothing of your own, not to touch a woman, to reside in the monastery under obedience to your superior, not to eat meat, and in the other outward matters of the discipline of the Rule to live according to monastic institution, unless with the greatest diligence you also strive to adorn your inner life through true charity toward God and neighbor. For charity is the end of regular observance, for the acquisition of which all the other things were principally instituted. Therefore without the charity of God all things profit you nothing, since it alone, and no other, distinguishes between good and evil works. O monk, monk, whoever you are who live lukewarmly in the monastery without the fervor of charity, do you think that the outward apparatus of discipline can save you? It is charity that sanctifies the one who has it; charity commends the other virtues and all good things to God. Have charity, and all the works of piety that you do will be pleasing to God.
Sermon IV.
On the difficult way that leads to life. Sermon IV.

You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ saying in today’s reading from the holy Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and confined the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” Is not Christ himself the way, who had said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? And how does he now say that it is confined and narrow, when he is the same one who had said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light”? What else is the yoke of Christ but the confined and narrow way to the kingdom of God? How then is it both light and narrow? Let your charity hear.

The yoke of the Lord Jesus is sweet to the good, but hard and unbearable to the reprobate. The way of Christ to life is broad and pleasant to the humble who are trained in charity, but narrow and bitter to the proud. For there is nothing so hard, nothing so terrible, nothing so difficult, that it is not easy and pleasant to one who loves God. Again, there is nothing so gentle, nothing so easy, nothing so small, that it is not heavy and burdensome to an evil will.

Therefore the Lord said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.” If you wish to carry my yoke upon you, first learn the meekness and humility of my heart; for unless you are meek and humble, you will by no means be able to carry my pack as if it were a heavy weight and an unbearable burden. I am a humble way to the proud; I am a narrow gate; I do not admit the swollen with pride. Unless you despise in your mind all things that are worldly, unless you bring necessary force against the pleasures of the flesh, you cannot enter through me into the kingdom like an animal loaded with sins. I am the humble way, and I receive the meek and humble. I am the narrow door; I admit the poor in spirit and the pure in heart.

To eternal life, brothers, we make our way by the narrow way of truth; therefore we must procure in due time all the things necessary for so difficult a journey. Now there are four things especially necessary for travelers, without which the journey is dangerous and the goal is rarely reached. The first thing that we say is necessary for travelers, we believe to be knowledge of the roads. For one who tries to walk far without prior knowledge of the roads is sometimes entangled in dangerous errors. Therefore let the prudent traveler either first learn the way, or take for himself an experienced companion for the journey, lest he either fall into the hands of robbers or depart from the right path of the journey.

Therefore, since we desire to return to the homeland of the heavenly kingdom by a way exceedingly narrow and known to few, it is necessary that we have as guide and companion of the journey Jesus Christ himself, who called himself the way and the truth. Outside Christ there is no true knowledge; and whoever neglects to have Christ as the companion of his journey runs in vain and without fruit. Therefore let us learn the way of life, dearly beloved brothers, without knowledge of which [unclear].

No one reaches the homeland, no one will attain eternal life. Let us firmly believe that our Lord Jesus Christ is the one mediator between God and human beings, true God and true man; outside faith in him no one will be saved, however innocently he may seem to live. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life abiding in himself. But he who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him.” What does “the wrath remains upon him” mean, except that the first original sin is not removed from him? For after the institution of the New Testament, original sin is removed from those who believe in him through faith in Christ alone. Circumcision was given to the fathers as a sign of future salvation; yet none of them could enter the kingdom of heaven before Christ the Savior rose from the dead. Therefore outside faith in Christ there is no salvation, since, as he himself said, whoever does not believe is already judged and will be condemned.

Let us remain in Christ through faith and love, for he is the way of salvation, he is truth without error, he is life without death. If we have the Lord Jesus as the guide of our journey, we walk with confidence. Secondly, it is necessary for travelers to pass through the lands of their journey without injury to anyone; for if they commit theft, robbery, or any other similar sin against the commonwealth, they would at last come to be punished with the ultimate penalty and would not reach the intended destination of their journey. But we, brothers, placed on the road by which we strive toward the homeland of the heavenly kingdom, must most carefully beware lest we commit anything by word, deed, or thought contrary to the justice of God; rather, let us render to each his right and his due: first to God, piety, worship, and charity; to our neighbor, love; to ourselves, the holiness of perfect purity. Indeed, if we live otherwise than Christ taught, we do not remain on the right way of salvation, which leads to the kingdom. But we shall remain on the way if we keep the commandments of God. We shall walk in truth if we love the Lord our God himself with the whole strength of our mind. We shall attain life if, turning away from evil, we continually persevere in the practice of good.

Thirdly, it is necessary to have provision for the journey, because if travelers’ supplies fail, they will not be able to reach the place intended. A prudent traveler, before he leaves his house, calculates for himself the length and difficulty of the journey, and according as necessity requires, prepares provisions and expenses. A great and arduous journey remains for us; therefore we must prepare supplies for many years, lest we fail on this road by which we are going. The provision for this journey of ours to the super-heavenly homeland is not gold, not silver, not the deceptive riches of the world, but faith in Christ and love of God. The holy virtues are an unfailing provision of the soul for the kingdom of heaven; strengthened by them, it walks the way of God in gladness. The soul faithful to Christ, and accompanied by the holy virtues, joyfully completes the arduous road of this long pilgrimage.

To love God above all things, to exercise oneself continually in good works, to keep one’s conscience in all purity, and to do injury to no one provides the soul with true provision for the journey to its everlasting homeland in heaven.

Fourth, travelers are necessarily advised not to forget the purpose they have undertaken before they reach the end of the journey. For he must be called a foolish traveler who is called back from his road by children’s games and forgets where he had meant to go. And we, dearest brothers, who have taken up the way of monastic religion, must always keep our end in mind, because even when we do not notice it, death hastens daily and presents both the unprepared and the prepared alike for judgment.

Meanwhile let us do good, while we may, as much as we can, and let us not delay turning to the Lord with our whole heart. Christ is the way by which we go to the kingdom of God. Christ is the truth, in which, if we remain, we do not go astray. Christ is the life for which we hope. Hear, brothers, what he himself says in the holy Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” This is the way upon which you entered from the beginning of your monastic profession. If you wish to proceed on it rightly and praiseworthily, you must live purely in regular observance and love Christ above all things. It is yours, brothers, to love nothing in this world and to chastise the flesh for the love of God. It belongs to monks to despise all the delights and pleasures of the present life and to desire nothing but the eternal banquet. It belongs to monks to imitate Christ with all their strength and to shape their life according to evangelical purity. To imitate Christ is the highest perfection. The faithful minister of Christ follows his Lord; and where Christ is, there also will his minister be. Therefore whoever among you loves his own salvation and desires to come after Christ to the kingdom of heaven, whoever wishes to guard and preserve to the end the things he promised on entering religion, let him also keep these things.

First of all, as far as he is able, let the monk learn through faith and devotion to know God in sincerity of mind, and at all times to occupy himself piously and soberly in the holy Scriptures. Whatever holy mother Church of the faithful has established either to be believed or to be observed, let him faithfully and firmly both believe and keep, and let him in no way depart from her determination. The flood once destroyed all who had remained outside the ark; Noah alone, with those who were in the ark, escaped safe. The ark presented the figure of the Church, and the deed that was done prefigured a mystery. Hence there is no salvation for men outside the Church, which our Lord Jesus Christ built upon the firmest rock. Every unbeliever is not in the Church, and therefore will necessarily perish, as once did those who were not in the ark. For all who do not believe in the Lord and Savior of the world, Jesus Christ, Jews, pagans, Gentiles, Saracens, likewise heretics and schismatics, who have withdrawn themselves from the unity of the Catholic Church, are placed outside the ark of salvation; and if they persevere in error, they are without doubt to be damned forever with the demons.

Since, then, faith is the foundation of salvation, without which it is impossible to please God, the monk must know what he ought to believe; and lest he happen to go astray, let him learn the Gospel and the constitutions of the Church that concern him. For he who is ignorant will be unknown. It is most shameful for a monk not to know the rules of the Christian faith, and to be utterly ignorant of what he is bound to believe for salvation. We do not say that the things proposed to you for belief should be examined by curious argument, since, as the holy Pope Gregory says, faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof for it. But we admonish you in this: that a monk ought to be studious in the divine Scriptures, so that he may know what holy mother Church commands him to believe, and may be able to guard against all errors contrary to the faith. Therefore let every monk, as a soldier of Jesus Christ, be firm and steadfast in the Catholic faith; let him be sober and studious in the Scriptures, and constant in good works.

The second thing which we believe to be necessary for a monk walking on the way of eternal salvation is that he strive to know himself. For self-knowledge is the best of all sciences, and therefore deservedly to be preferred to all the pursuits of mortals. Yet the beginning of this saving knowledge is exceedingly difficult, because there are very few who do not love the world. For everyone who follows the world and loves the vanities that pass away cannot be one who knows himself. And nothing hinders a man more from knowledge of himself than man himself. He who is fed on the pleasures of his flesh, who is lifted up into pride by the vain knowledge of this world, or by riches, or by honors, is not permitted to come to knowledge of himself. Nevertheless, to know many things and to neglect oneself is not wisdom, but rather madness. It belongs to the heap of a heavier damnation to learn many things and shamefully to be ignorant of oneself.

Let each of you therefore consider what he is, whence he is, and what he is going to be. Man, certainly, of himself is nothing; but whatever he is, he is from God and for God. What is man but a traveler and a pilgrim, as it were of one day upon the earth, who today is seen alive in the world, but in the morning, snatched away by death, is seen no more? All our life, every action, every day, every hour, shows how nothing we are: we die by living, are corrupted by acting, are extinguished with time, and are changed. O tearful race of men, unstable, miserable, and weak, how windy, blind, and vain I see you to be, when I make a comparison between ourselves in the present and those who have gone before us to death. He spoke truly who compared you to the leaf of a tree. The wind, snatching a leaf from the tree, casts it to the ground; in its place another new leaf afterwards grows up, subject to a like fall. But what has fallen to the ground is resolved into the earth, and never thereafter returns to the tree. Hence a certain wise man of the Greeks says:
As is the race of leaves, so also is the race of men.
The race of men is very like the race of leaves, because it grows green for a time and is resolved into the earth; and neither does the leaf return to the tree, nor man to life.

Now follows the third thing, which I think very necessary for a monk walking in the way of God. Every man who understands himself to be a traveler in this life of very brief duration truly shows himself humble in all things. For why should earth and ashes be proud? He who truly knows himself cannot be exalted. My brothers, we have no cause for exaltation and pride, but much and continual cause for humility, since we are earth, a certain compacting of dust, and after a few days are to return again into dust. But because true humility belongs to few, therefore the way of salvation is called narrow and is found by few. By humility one comes to the kingdom, because, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel, everyone who humbles himself for God’s sake will be exalted, and he who exalts himself will be humbled.

Fourth, for the monk traveling to heaven it is supremely necessary that he make himself a stranger to every sin, because no one is admitted into the kingdom of God unless he is commended by the highest purity of conscience. Therefore the conscience must continually be adorned with holy virtues and good works, because heaven is opened only to those who despise the world for love of God. Hence Peter, the most holy chief apostle of Christ, says in his second epistle: Applying all care, minister virtue in your faith; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, abstinence; in abstinence, patience; in patience, godliness; in godliness, love of brotherhood; and in love of brotherhood, charity. If these things are present with you and abound, they will make you neither empty nor without fruit in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. There is one virtue, as Firmianus testifies, and one way of the good, which leads and carries souls stripped of the flesh not into the fabulous Elysian fields of the poets, but into the choirs of angels: namely, the Christian faith adorned by works of true charity, which flees every sin.

Fifth, the traveler on the steep road of the heavenly kingdom is instructed that, by keeping God’s will, he should follow the commandments in all things. Whatever he is about to say or do, let him first examine diligently whether it agrees with the ordinances of God and of the Church. But if he finds it contrary either to God or to the Church, let him flee from it at once, lest he fall into sin. For it belongs to a wise man to commit nothing unexamined, but to consider all things diligently by the counsel of foresight before he acts. But whoever wishes to be safe and secure on this steep journey should, to the best of his strength, imitate the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the light for all unto eternal life.

The sixth thing that we judge necessary for our traveler is that he love the saving study of Scripture. Let him not be curious in reading, nor given to vain superstitions, but simple, pure, and upright in soul. It does not befit a monk to cling to writings.

of the gentiles, nor devote his study to the fables of shameful poets. He who follows vain things will never be wise; and he who seeks out curious matters will quickly fall into sin. The monk should always avoid every reading of vain superstition; and whatever does not contribute to knowledge of the divine Scriptures must at all times be despised by our traveler.

Seventh, we judge it very necessary for our traveler that he prudently direct both his senses and his thoughts, and guard them from every disordered desire. Our stubborn little ass must be restrained by the bridle of discipline, lest it cast its rider, the spirit, headlong into hell. He who always considers that he walks in the sight of him who sees all things preserves his conscience pure and clean with the greatest diligence. He always keeps watch in the fear of the Lord; always, in fasting and abstinence, he chastises his poor little body for love of the heavenly homeland. The monk who knows himself to be a pilgrim and a stranger in this world never forgets the heavenly homeland, because he sees nothing on the road of this present life in which his soul may take delight. For the prudent traveler pays no attention to the spectacles along the roads; nothing among passing things delights him in his pilgrimage, but at all times he sighs for the end of the journey. He always thinks of the sweet homeland, he bears it heavily that his pilgrimage is prolonged or delayed, and therefore he desires to have nothing in this world except the Lord Jesus, into whose presence he eagerly hastens to appear.

Eighth, tireless practice of divine charity is necessary for our traveler. For no one will be able to come to the heavenly homeland who departs from the path of charity. The charity of God is the way to God; if anyone has neglected to have it burning within himself, he has miserably strayed from the true road of the heavenly homeland. God, says Scripture, is charity, and he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. But he who is not in charity has already withdrawn far from the way of salvation, and, walking in the darkness of sins, will never come to the kingdom.
How Sin Must Be Fled. Sermon V.

You have all heard, my dearly beloved brothers, what Saint John the Apostle said about sinners: He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil sins from the beginning. A sentence to be feared and greatly dreaded. If all who commit sin are of the devil, and we all offend in many things, how many shall we find immune from sin? Nevertheless he says immediately after: Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he is born of God. But he had said before: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. What is the meaning of this contradiction: that none of the sons of God is without sin, and yet he who is born of God does not commit sin?
Sermon V.

There is no contradiction found here, since both statements are true: no one is without sin, in that no one is without the law of sin; and he who is born of God does not commit sin, because through the law of the mind, that is, through charity, which is the seed of God, he does not commit sin. For charity covers a multitude of sins; without it there is no good work, and it alone has power to blot out every sin. Hence the holy bishop Augustine says: No saint and no just man is without sin; yet on account of this he does not cease to be just or holy, if he holds fast to holiness with affection. But these sins of the just are not to be regarded as mortal or enormous, but as small and venial sins, without which the present life is scarcely lived; for every mortal sin must be far from the just man, if he is to retain the name of justice.

For mortal sin separates man from God, kills the soul, and condemns it eternally with the demons. By the grace of God we can avoid this destructive kind of mortal sin, and through uprightness of will we must do so diligently. For this is why we have been made monks: that, living most cautiously under the command of saving obedience, we might not fall into the pit of mortal sin. Therefore a monk must always keep watch in good works, so that he may live free from mortal crime.

But whoever, on the way of God, feels his flesh troublesome and contrary to him must make it subject to the spirit through remembrance of punishments, and obedient, as it were, through fear. First of all, then, a monk who loves his own salvation should always attentively consider the deceitful condition of this world and its deception, and should weigh how quickly every delight of the flesh passes away. He can easily draw his soul away from sins who has carefully considered that the pleasure of the flesh is very brief, but the punishment owed to sinners is eternal.

The world passes away, and its desire with it; all human beings too pass away by dying, and no one is permitted to remain long in this life. For what is the world but a great sea, deep and restless? In it there are as many creeping things of evils as there are evil desires of human beings [unclear]. O deceitful, deceiving, and unclean world, you shamefully deceive those who cling to you; you plunge all who follow you into the depth of hell. How happy are those who despise you for love of Christ, and, making a useful separation from your vanities, depart from you in time.

Whatever we see in the world is vain, and every lover of the world becomes vain and will soon be corrupted. Think that you will soon die, for nothing draws a person back from sin as frequent and intent meditation on death does. For Scripture says: Remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Thought of the necessity of dying shakes the mind with fear and restrains it from vice.

The second thing that persuades one to flee sin is fear of the future judgment, at which all human beings must necessarily be presented. No one can escape this terrible judgment; rather, we must all appear at it. Two things must be feared by us.

Two judgments are impending, neither of which we shall be able to escape; rather, necessity compels us to appear at both. One is called the particular judgment, in which, immediately after death, the soul is judged according to its merits, either to grace or to punishment. The other is named the general judgment, which will be at the end of the age, where we shall all be judged publicly by the only-begotten Son of God.

Both judgments are exceedingly terrible and greatly to be feared by all mortals. Hence the prophet Joel says: “Great is the day of the Lord, and very terrible; and who shall endure it?” Likewise in Ecclesiastes King Solomon says: “All things that are done under the sun God will bring into judgment, judging every error, whether it be good or evil.” In Isaiah also it is read thus: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes.” And in the book of the prophet Amos it is written: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord. What is it to you? For that day of the Lord is darkness and not light.” Zephaniah also, the prophet of the Lord, foretelling the bitterness of the future judgment, said: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind.
